MOTIONS
Ombudsmen, Office—50th Anniversary of Establishment

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Following discussion in the
Business Committee, I seek leave to move G overnment motion No. 1. I move that this
House place on record—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I had better put that leave to the House. Leave is sought for
that purpose. Is there any objection? There is no objection.

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: I move, That this House place on record that 1 October
marks the 50 th anniversary of the establishment of the Office of Ombudsmen in New
Zealand, the first in an English-speaking country and a model for the spread of the
office throughout the world, and note the important contribution that the office makes to
the preservation of administrative justice in this country.
The Government is pleased to recognise the 50 th anniversary of the establishment of
the Office of the Ombudsmen. The concept originated in Sweden in the early 19 th
century. The Swedish Ombudsmen had juri sdiction over almost all national and
municipal officials, who could be discip lined and even prosecuted for incorrect
behaviour. Champions for establishing th e Ombudsman in New Zealand included
National Party politicians John, or Jack, Marshall and Ralph Hanan.
The Office of the Ombudsmen in New Zealand was established under the
Parliamentary Commissioner (Ombudsman)  Act 1962 as an independent office
protected by the authority of Parliament. This set an international precedent as in other
countries Ombudsmen were appointed by th e Government. The first Ombudsman, Sir
Guy Powles, a former lawyer, soldier, and diplomat, was sworn in  on 1 October 1962.
He held the office until 1977. His performan ce made the institution widely respected,
and its authority and scope were extended. The Ombudsmen Act 1975 allowed the
appointment of several Ombudsmen, and thei r jurisdiction was ex tended to statutory
boards and local government. Successive le gislation has solidified the Ombudsmen’s
position. The 1982 Official Information Act,  the 1987 Local Government Official
Information and Meetings Act, the Prot ected Disclosures Ac t 2000, and the Crown
Entities Act 2004 have all added to the transparency of governing.
New Zealand has been blessed to have had a succession of successful and influential

items.speaker: Ombudsmen
items.text: Sir Guy Powles, Sir George Laking, Eaton Hurley, Lester Castle, Sir John
Robertson, Nadja Tollemache, who was New Zealand’s first Ombudswoman, Susan
Richards, Sir Brian Elwood, the Rt Hon Sir Anand Satyanand, Mel Smith, John
Belgrave, and the two current Ombudsmen, Dame Beverley Wakem and David McGee.
So on this 50 th anniversary we congra tulate them on all they do for New Zealand, and
we look forward to the next 50 years.

items.speaker: CHARLES CHAUVEL
items.text: Since its creation half a century ago, the Office
of the Ombudsmen has been occupied by a nu mber of truly gifted New Zealanders. The
Deputy Leader of the House named them, a nd many of those names resonate with us
still: Powles, our last Governor of Samoa; Laking, our ambassador to Washington in the
years of the Kennedy and Johnson administrati ons; Robertson, a former State Services
Commissioner, Secretary of De fence, and Secretary for Justice; Satyanand, a District
Court judge who would go on to be Governor -General; Smith, a former Secretary for
Justice; Belgrave, a former Secretary for Ju stice and also Secretary of Commerce, State
5738 Motions 27 Sep 2012
Services Commissioner, and Comptroller of  Customs; McGee, a long-serving and
distinguished Clerk of this House; and, last, but of course not leas t, Wakem, previously
Chief Executive of Radio New Zealand an d a member of the Higher Salaries
Commission. These have all been  Officers of Parliament of  significant stature, who
have served the public and our Parliament with distinction since 1962.
The Ombudsmen perform an extremely impor tant role. As we look forward to the
work of the office over the next 50 years we must all take seriously our responsibility as
parliamentarians to ensure that it is properly resourced to do its job, and that we treat the
office and its staff with the respect and the compliance that  the law properly demands.
The Labour Opposition is pleased to support the motion.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia ora. I rise to
support the motion on the 50 th anniversary of the establishment of the Office of the
Ombudsmen. When New Zealand’s first Ombuds man, Sir Guy Powles, was sworn in in
front of the Speaker of Parliament in 1962, he said “The Ombudsman is Parliament’s
person—put there for the protection of the in dividual,”. New Zealand was the fourth
country, after Sweden, Finland, and Denm ark, to establish the Office of the
Ombudsmen, and was the first country outside of  Scandinavia. It is an idea that has
caught on, and now, according to the International Ombudsman Institute, there are more
than 150 countries with Ombudsmen-like institutions around the world.
We would like to acknowledge the work of all the Ombudsmen, including the current
two, Dame Beverley Wakem and Dr David Mc Gee, and also all the staff who have
worked for them over the years. They play an important role in our democracy.
However, we would also like to note the importance of adequate funding for them to
be able to do that important role. In th e 2011 financial review of the Office of the
Ombudsmen, the Chief Ombudsman stated that the office was in crisis and was now
handling a significant increase in workloa d. We share what the member Charles
Chauvel has said about the responsibility of all in Parliament to adequately fund the
office.
We have not agreed with every deci sion made by the Ombudsmen, and probably
Governments have agreed even less, which I guess is testimony to the independence of
the office. But I would like to share one positive example. In 2009 councils in Tasman
and Canterbury were refusing to release im portant information regarding thousands of
potentially contaminated toxic sites. As a result of the action by the Ombudsmen, that
information is now public. We believe it was the right call, a nd it would not have
happened without the intervention of the Ombudsmen. Fifty years on, we would like to
acknowledge the establishment of this important office. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: New Zealand First joins with
other parties in acknowledgi ng the celebration of this 50 th anniversary of the
establishment of the Office of the Ombudsmen.  As has been said, to be correct, New
Zealand was the first country outside of S candinavia to establish an Office of the
Ombudsmen. Since then, the Office of the Om budsmen has come to play a significant
role in our democracy.
How ironic it is that we are marking this event this week. Thomas Jefferson said that
the price of freedom is eternal vigilance. Th is week we have had a perfect illustration
through the revelations of unlawful surv eillance activity of the Government
Communications Security Bureau of the im portance of ensuring open, transparent, and
accountable Government. We have been re minded that the great est threat to our
democracy is secrecy and the abuse of power that occurs when the public are denied
their right to know. Once again we have seen that those in  power are given to ignoring
due process and the law, and that an effec tive democracy requires a range of supporting
structures and institutions.
27 Sep 2012 Motions 5739
The Office of the Ombudsmen has proven a powerful mechanism for keeping the
public informed, but there is a deeply tr oubling tendency for Government to apply
obfuscation and delay in respond ing to Official Information Act requests, and all of us
around here have been privy to  that. New Zealand First cons iders there is a strong case
that additional funding should be allocated to  the Office of the Ombudsmen to ensure
the public can gain access to official inform ation without the inordi nate delay that is
often now the case. And probably the same sh ould be said about the Neazor report and
that office, as well.
It is appropriate that we mark the 50 th anniversary of the esta blishment of the Office
of the Ombudsmen, because it plays a vital ro le in supporting democratic processes in
New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon PETER DUNNE
items.text: On behalf of United Future, I
want to associate myself with the remarks that  have been made by others to first of all
recognise and secondly congratulate the Offi ce of the Ombudsmen on the attainment of
its 50th anniversary.
When the office was established in 1962, times were much simpler, and the notion
that there should be some sort of independent watchdo g able to ca ll Government
agencies to account for actions where the in dividual citizen felt aggrieved was a pretty
attractive one. For the first 20 years of th e office’s existence, that was largely its
primary function. But the role of th e Office of the Ombudsmen has changed
significantly since the advent of the Offici al Information Act, and the Ombudsman has
become much more of an arbi ter of decisions as to whether or not certain information
should be released. I often fear that that may be to the cost of the individual citizen. The
aggrieved small person who wanted to take  an action before the Ombudsman may now
find that the pressure from other claims, usua lly associated with Official Information
Act requests in and around Government, is re ducing that authority. I am not saying that
the two are inconsistent. I guess I am supporting the role of the office and the need for it
to be resourced to do the job.
Finally, can I conclude by no ting the high calibre of peopl e who have served in the
role of Chief Ombudsman over the years. I have  had the privilege of working at various
times with every one of them, bar Sir Guy Powles, and I think that they have all brought
a uniformly high standard of integrity, intell igence, and perspicacity to the role. At the
end of the day, what has made this office the success it has been, aped by so many other
countries around the world but also now a revered New Zealand institution, has been the
calibre of people who have served in that ro le. I think the challenge for this Parliament
in the future when it appoints the next round of  Ombudspeople is to make sure that that
consistently high standard is maintained and developed, and that the office in its next 50
years continues to receive the respect that it deserves from the citizens of New Zealand.
Motion agreed to.
Sir John Wallace, KNZM, QC

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion
without notice on the passing of Sir John Wallace, who, as you know, was the Chief
Human Rights Commissioner, a High Court judge, and the chairman of the royal
commission on the electoral reform structure that we now have.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.

items.speaker: Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS
items.text: I move, That this House note the passing of Sir John
Wallace KNZM, QC, former Chief Human Ri ghts Commissioner, judge of the High
5740 Obituaries 27 Sep 2012
Court of New Zealand, and chairman of the Royal Commission on the Electoral System,
which recommended the MMP system for se lecting elected members of Parliament . On
behalf of New Zealand First, I wish to pay respects and to mark the passing of an
eminent and distinguished New Zealander. Sir John made an outstanding contribution to
public office in New Zealand in all the role s he fulfilled with distinction. As chairman
of the Royal Commission on the Elec toral System, which recommended the
introduction of MMP, Sir John made a lasting and profound difference to our
parliamentary system and democracy. We extend our condolences to Sir John’s family.
Motion agreed to.

Tabling of Documents—Accuracy of Description of Documents

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr
Speaker. It is in respect of  the tabling of documents. As  you know, we have discussed
whether or not Speakers’ ruli ngs 147(4), (5), and (6) are being followed when there is
the injection of commentary into the tabling of  documents. I raise this in respect of the
documents tabled by the senior Opposition wh ip yesterday in response to an oral
question to the Minister of Education, wh ere he paraphrased, and I quote—I will not
quote exactly, but it is basically suggesting that  the Minister’s time frame would be 5 to
6 weeks. On analysing the document when it was tabled, it eventuated that neither was
it the Minister’s time frame nor was it in  respect of merger s and closures in
Christchurch, but, in fact, of the special education review that was under way. I do not
want to suggest to the House that the Oppositi on whip misled the House, or, if he did,
that it was intentional, but I raise it as an example of the risks involved in the
commentary that goes around the tabling of documents, and I would ask that you would
again review that, with a view to curtailing the commentary that is attached to the leave
that is sought.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the point that is being ra ised is an interesting one. I ask
members, naturally, to say sufficient about th e document to enable the House to make a
rational decision about whether members shoul d allow it to be tabled. But I think the
point is well made that that should not include  going into great detail of what is in the
document. Members must be careful when they indicate what is in the document. I think
members need to have some idea of what is in the document in order to make a decision
about whether it should be tabled, but the need  for absolute accuracy  there is crucial.
Seeking leave to table a document is an action of some formality. Members have
27 Sep 2012 Points of Order 5741
thought about the desire to seek leave. The House considers the matter, and gives leave.
It is an important process. Therefore, careful thought should be given by members when
they do indicate what is in a document.
Job Creation—Statistics and Reports
1. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance :
How many jobs have been created in th e New Zealand economy over the past two
years?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance: Mr Speaker—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Order! I apologise to the Minister. The question contains no
assertions of fact. It just asks a straight question. Before  the Minister had even opened
his mouth, there was totally unacceptable interjection.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: A net 57,000 more New Zealande rs have a job now than 2
years ago. That is according to the household labour force survey, seasonally adjusted,
which is the standard internationally recognised measure of employment and
unemployment.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What examples has he seen of jobs being created in the
infrastructure sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Thanks to the Government’s  multibillion-dollar investment
in infrastructure, afte r years of under-investment, and als o, of course, the Christchurch
rebuild, many projects are bei ng undertaken to help crea te a faster-growing economy.
Some specific examples include 1,000 new jobs over the next 4 years with the
Waterview Connection construction, 1,000 new c onstruction jobs at Wiri Prison, nearly
2,000 people in employment thanks to the ro ll-out of ultra-fast  broadband, and 1,000
employed on the horizontal infrastructure re build in Christchurc h. Together, the total
construction workforce required for the wide r Canterbury rebuild is estimated to be
around 32,000.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What examples has he seen of jobs being created in the
manufacturing and information and communications technology sectors?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The manufacturing sector has grown 6.1 percent by volume
in the 2 years to June 2012. Some specific exam ples of jobs in this sector include the
Continuous Catalyst Regeneration Project —which is just about to commence—at
Marsden Point, which will employ around 350 people; the recommissioning of the
second train at Methanex’s methanol plant in Taranaki, which has involved up to 500
jobs; and the new, $200 million Fonterra plant at Darfield, which has involved more
than 1,500 people during its construction. In the information and communications
technology sector, examples include 400 new jobs in a pa rtnership between IBM and
Unitec, 128 new jobs at Xero this calendar year, more than 100 new jobs at software
company Orion Health, plus jobs at othe r great New Zealand exporting organisations
like Tait Communications, Oktobor Animation, and many more.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Has he seen any other examples of  projects that would create jobs
that have not yet been able to proceed?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Minister has seen some examples of that. For example,
a new international convention centre in Auckland would create around a thousand new
jobs during its construction and around 800 jobs once it is up and running. Of course,
that is being opposed as much as possibl e and slowed down by the Greens and Labour.
Then there is the Bathurst Resources escarpment mine project on the West Coast, which
5742 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012
would employ 225 people, if objectors withdrew  their appeals, of course. I would say
again to the Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union, Labour, and
the Greens that if they were serious about  helping Coasters, th ey would call on
opponents to drop their objections and allow this project to proceed.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: What reports has he seen about  support for jobs in the mining
sector?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Minister has seen three quite intriguing reports. The
first, a recent statement, sa id “Let me be very clear here, I have always supported
mining on the West Coast.”, the second said that “undeveloped coal reserves should be
left in the ground.”, and the third said th at “Our position on mining has never been
unclear and has always been consistent.” Those three statements came from Labour
MPs Damien O’Connor, Maryan Street, and David Parker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Trevor Mallard. [ Interruption] Order! I want to hear this
question. The Hon Trevor Mallard.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Has he seen the letter from Or ion Health—which he referred
to in a supplementary answer—to Craig Foss, the Minister of Commerce, indicating that
its business had been placed at risk as a re sult of the decision of Mr Foss to override the
unanimous decision of a select  committee of this House to  do with the patenting of
software, and that its business could well go offshore as a result of that?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, I am not aware of a letter in that regard. I suggest that
if the member has a question in that respec t he puts it down to Mr Foss, who is in
charge of that portfolio. Also, from my br ief knowledge of the matter that the member
raises, I do not think his assertion is correct, anyway.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table a document compiled by the Parliamentary
Library, which shows that th ere are more New Zealanders  unemployed as of June 2012
than there were in June 2010.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any
objection? There is objection.
Question time interrupted.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I seek leave to correct a
misrepresentation that has just been made—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Is the member seeking leave to make a personal
explanation?

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Yes, that is right, to correct  a misrepresentation made by the

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think we have got to be a little  careful here. We have got to be a

There is a procedure about that.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I think the difficulty we have is that the senior Government whip

I have now had the opportunity to consult the document that I tabled yesterday, and it

27 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5743

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is now, by way of  a point of order, trying to—I
think if the member is going to exclusively speak about his situati on, I am prepared to

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: Yesterday in question time I s ought leave to table a document,
and I paraphrased from the document what I believed that it contained. The document
is, in fact, itself a series of  paraphrases of the discussion that took place at a meeting
that was run by the Ministry of Education, a nd therefore it does not necessarily follow a
logical flow. Questions were raised regarding special education, but questions were also
raised regarding the time frame that schools would be required to take. For the benefit
of the House, I quote directly from the document, which I did not do yesterday but I will
do now: “The advice from National Offi ce regarding the likely timeframe for
community consultation was that a r ecommendation would go to the Minister
suggesting five to six weeks.” The following paragraph then goes on to say that if the
board decided it needed more time or the Minister decided it needed more time, there
can be a further 28-day period. I am of th e understanding, from people who were at the
meeting, and from the context of the rest of the document, that that does not, in fact,
refer to special education but refers to the—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member is now starting to debate what was said by
another member. I think he has made his position fairly clear in the personal explanation

Question time resumed.
Dotcom Case—Role of Government Security Agencies
2. GRANT ROBERTSON (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Prime Minister :
When was his Chief of Staff first informed  about the role of the GCSB in the Kim
Dotcom case, and when were officials from  the Department of Prime Minister and
Cabinet, including the Intelligence Co-o rdination Group, the National Assessments
Bureau, and the Security Intelligence Service first aware of the Kim Dotcom case?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Economic Development) on behalf of the

items.speaker: Prime Minister
items.text: The Prime Minister’s chief of staff was first informed of the role that
the Government Communications Security Bureau played on Monday, 17 September.
He had been alerted the previo us Thursday that there was a potential issue of illegality
relating to an operation that the Govern ment Communications Security Bureau had
conducted in relation to Kim Do tcom, but at that time was given no details of the role
the Government Communications Security Bu reau had played. Hi s office advised the
Government Communications Security Bureau th at the director needed to directly brief
the Prime Minister as quickly as possible face to face. That meeting was arranged prior
to the end of the week and took place on Monday, 17 September, following Cabinet. I
am advised that there was no involvement by any Department of the Prime Minister and
Cabinet agency prior to the arrest of Ki m Dotcom. With regard to the Security
Intelligence Service, I am advised that its involvement was limited to routine checks,
which were made when Dotcom applied for New Zealand residency in 2010.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. I appreciate that that was a
detailed question, and I also appreciate th e Minister’s answer. In respect of the
Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet,  all he told us there was that it had no
5744 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012
knowledge prior to the arrest. That does not really answer the question of when it was
first aware.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the Minister has gone to some trouble to answer the question
with some particularity. When I read the quest ion I made notes of th e first part of the
question—that the Minister should give a precise answer to that, because it is something
that there should be a clear answer to. Th e second part of the question, asking when
those various agencies were aware, is a matter that is far more vague. I think it would be
difficult for me to try to pin the Minister down on that when there are further
supplementary questions available. I think the Minister has made a pretty reasonable fist
of answering that question.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he confirm, in light of that answer, that his chief of staff did
in fact find out about the Government Comm unications Security Bureau’s role on the
Thursday before 17 September, not on 17 September as he told the House yesterday?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I can only repeat what I said in the first answer, which was
that the chief of staff had b een alerted the previous Thursd ay that there was a potential
issue of illegality relating to an opera tion that the Government Communications
Security Bureau had conducted in relation to Kim Dotcom. But at that time he was
given no details of the role that the Government Communica tions Security Bureau had
played.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: When—on what date—did the Depart ment of the Prime Minister
and Cabinet become aware of the Kim Dotcom case?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am advised there was no involvement by any Department
of the Prime Minister and Cabinet agency pr ior to the arrest of Kim Dotcom. I presume
they read the newspapers at some point.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he think that ignorance of the law by the Government
Communications Security Bureau and the polic e is an acceptable reason for what has
occurred?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Prime Minister has rel eased a press release this
afternoon that indicates his concern and disappointment at the actions of the
Government Communications Security Bureau and at the errors that have been made,
and that is clearly laid out. There is also an associated statement from the director of the
Government Communications Security Bureau, in terms of the actions it will be taking.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he think that Justice Neazo r is conflicted in reviewing the
actions of the Government Communications Secu rity Bureau in this case, given that his
normal role involves monitoring and worki ng with the Government Communications
Security Bureau, and is he in effect investigating his own actions here?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the role of Justice Neazor—who, I would point out,
is a former Solicitor-General and a former j udge of the High Court— is exactly the role
that he has undertaken in doing this inquiry for the Prime Minister.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he think that New Zealanders have a right to expect more of
him as the Minister responsible for our securi ty agencies than the casual, disinterested
approach he has taken to this case?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I completely reject that as sertion. The Prime Minister was
advised and had the meeting on 17 September,  and promptly called an inquiry, which
has now been released today. It is pathetic to suggest that he was disinterested.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: What was discussed in the 15 m eetings that the Prime Minister
had with the Government Communications Security Bureau this year if it was not about
cases that involve the United States Govern ment, the FBI, and a range of New Zealand
agencies?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: In so far as the Minister is ab le to answer, I call the Hon Steven
Joyce.
27 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5745

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Firstly, obviously, those are ma tters of national security.
But, secondly, the member seems to be suggesting that the Pr ime Minister would
involve himself in the operati onal control on a day-to-day ba sis of security services.
That is a particularly disturbing—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. Order! The member asked a question that perhaps there was
no way the Minister could answer, but that doe s not mean that the Minister goes on to
that sort of material.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he accept that as Minister responsible for the Government
Communications Security Bureau he acts as the main democratic check for New
Zealanders on our security agencies, and should he not be taking his role more seriously
than to have 15 meetings where apparently  he was not briefed about one of these
operations?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I appreciate Mr Robertson is trying to obfuscate in this
matter, but the reality is the Prime Minister  was made aware on 17 September, and then
called an inquiry.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he take responsibility for the actions of the Government
Communications Security Bureau, an ag ency for which he has ministerial
responsibility?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The Prime Minister, of course, is the Minister responsible
for the Government Communications Security Bureau, and as soon as the matters were
raised with him, he called an inquiry. Th at inquiry has been announced today. It is
exactly the right thing to do, and the me mber is being disingenuous by suggesting
anything else.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, if that is the Prime Minister’s answer, is he aware
that the inspector-general is charged with also reviewing the manner in which the SIS
interception warrants are sought, that he a pproved the inspector-general to lead the
inquiry before he even ascertained whethe r the SIS was involved in the Dotcom case,
and is that not new evidence justifying a full- scale inquiry into the matter, covering all
departments and agencies involved in the case, in order to ascertain what has gone
wrong and restore the public’s faith in these institutions?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: That was a many-legged questi on. All I can say is that the
report of the inspector-general is on the ta ble today. It lays out clearly the mistakes
made by the Government Communications Secur ity Bureau and the actions to be taken
by it.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware that in the Inspector-General of
Intelligence and Security Annual Report 2011 , the inspector-general states specifically
that “In particular the [inspector-general] assists the Minister to ensure that the activities
of [the agencies] comply with the law”, and hence the inspector-general himself is
implicated in the failure of the Government  Communications Security Bureau to follow
the law, so having the inspector-general do the investigation is a conflict of interest?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I reject the member’s suppos ition, and I would point out
that the inspector-general has done exactly what  is required of him, which is to have an
inquiry into the matters that have been  raised in regard to the Government
Communications Security Bureau.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I seek leave to table this document. It is not available online. It
is very difficult to get hold of, actually. It is the Inspector-General of Intelligence and
Security Annual Report 2011, from which that quote came.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any objection?
There is no objection.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.
5746 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does the Prime Minister accept that the precedent for a Minister
who is responsible but not aw are of an issue comes from Denis Marshall in the Cave
Creek situation, where the Minister resigned?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I appreciate what the member is trying to do. It is the job of
a Minister to respond, as in this case, as soon as he was made aware of the situation, to
call an inquiry, which has reported today, and actions are now being taken to correct the
matters that have been identified.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware that under the Government
Communications Security Bureau Act 2003 ther e is a much higher level of ministerial
control required than of most  Government agencies, and th at section 8(3) says “The
performance of the Bureau’s functions is s ubject to the control of the Minister.”—that
is, the Minister has specific responsibilities around controlling the actions of the agency;
he cannot just take a hands-off approach?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am sure the member would understand that there is a fine
line between actually taking c ontrol of the day-to-day ope rations—and I think it would
be in fact a pretty disturbing suggestion that the Prime Minister would be required to do
that. The reality is that all Ministers are res ponsible for the actions of their departments,
and, when a department makes an error, to investigate that  error and take remedial
action. That is what has happened in this case.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware that under the Government
Communications Security Bureau Act the Mi nister in charge of the Government
Communications Security Bureau actually ha s to sign off personally the interception
warrants, which means that the Minister know s the names and identities of the people
who are having their communicat ions intercepted? There is  a much higher level of
ministerial intervention into the operational and day-to-day activities of the Government
Communications Security Bureau than for any other Government agency, the reason
being that there is no other democratic ove rsight of the Govern ment Communications
Security Bureau.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I would point out to the member again that in this instance
the Government Communications Security Bure au has made, as the Prime Minister has
identified, two errors. They have now been investigated and they were investigated
promptly once the Prime Minister was made aware of those two errors. Despite what the
member suggests, I think it is di fficult for any Minister to be aware of an error before it
has been brought to their attention.
Prisoners, Employment Training—Prisoner Skills and Employment Strategy and
Better Public Services Targets
3. JACQUI DEAN (National—Waitaki)  to the Minister of Corrections : What
were the results of the Prisoner Skills and Employment Strategy 2009-2012?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Targets set for prisoners engaged
in education and employment under the strate gy have been exceeded by more than 100
percent. During the course of the Prisone r Skills and Employ ment Strategy 2009-2012,
the number of prisoners in vocational trai ning, employment, and l iteracy and numeracy
education increased to 7,529 from 5,359, an in crease of 2,170, compared with the target
of 1,000. There has also been a 33 percent increa se in prisoners enrolled in literacy and
numeracy programmes, of  which 58 percent are M āori. All evidence shows that
prisoners who are released with improved skills are significantly less likely to reoffend.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: What are the next steps for the Department of Corrections to further
improve the numbers of prisoners engaged in employment and training?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: The Better Public Services targets for the Department of
Corrections will see a 25 percent reduction in reoffending by 2017. This will lead to 600
fewer prisoners and 4,000 fewer community offenders being reconvicted every year,
27 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5747
and 18,500 fewer victims every year. Over th e next 5 years nearly 3,000 additional
prisoners will be in education and empl oyment training, while 7,500 prisoners and
community offenders will be given support to find real jobs in ne w partnerships with
employers and industry.
Dotcom Case—Government Communications Security Bureau Actions and
Confidence in Minister
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Prime Minister: Does he
have confidence in the Minister for the G overnment Communications Security Bureau
(GCSB) given the Prime Minister’s statem ent that the GCSB unlawfully intercepted
communications in relation to Kim Dotcom; if so, why?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Economic Development)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Prime Minister
items.text: Yes; because as soon as the Minister  was made aware of the issues in
question he called for an urgent inquiry by the Inspector-General of Intelligence and
Security, and that inquiry report has been released publicly into the House today.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How can he be confident that the Minister responsible for the
GCSB is fulfilling his statutory functions to control the Government Communications
Security Bureau under section 8(3) of the Government Communications Security
Bureau Act, given that the Minister was unaware of the bureau’s involvement in the
Kim Dotcom case until last week—a case that began in December of last year?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is important to point out the outcome of the report, which
may assist the member with his—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: We know what the outcome is. Why didn’t he know?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If Mr Peters knew the outcome  he would know that that
question was not actually the correct interp retation. Firstly, there were two mistakes.
The Government Communications Security  Bureau originally relied on police
information about the residency status of the people in question; it did not check further.
Secondly, the error was compounded, after its operation was concluded, simply by a
wrong interpretation of the law. Those are two very significant erro rs that have been
identified in the report by the inspector-general. As the member will see, the
Government Communications Security Bureau  is taking action in regard to those
matters.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Before I call the member for hi s next question, the Minister’s
answer did not actually answer  the question that was aske d. The question asked about
the role of the Minister in relation to section 8(3) of the Act in respect of, as the member
asking the question alleges, the control of  the Government Communications Security
Bureau and how he sort of justifies that requirement of the Act—or how he lines up that
requirement of the Act against the claime d unawareness of any involvement of the
bureau since November last year, or some time. In order to clarify the situation—
because I do not want to destroy the memb er’s question—I think I should invite Dr
Russel Norman to repeat his question, becau se these are serious matters. The member
has not made any outrageous assertions in his question, at all. He has cited the Act. He
has asked how the member justifies what ha s happened, given the requirements of the
Act. I ask Dr Russel Norman to repeat his question.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How can he be confident that the Minister responsible for the
GCSB is fulfilling his statutory functions to control the Government Communications
Security Bureau under section 8( 3) of the relevant Act, give n that the Minister has told
us that he was unaware of the bureau’s invo lvement in the Kim Dotcom case until last
week—a case that began in December of last year?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think that a different way of  putting the answer is that the
Government Communications Security Bu reau was operating under the assumption, I
5748 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012
think, that it did not need to advise its Mi nister, because of its interpretation of the
residency status of the person involved. Obviously that has proven to be incorrect.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: How can he be confident in th e Minister’s ov ersight of the
Government Communications Security Bu reau when the inspector-general of
Intelligence and Security, in  his annual report of 2011, ra ised concerns about the
operation of Government Communications Secur ity Bureau authorisations to intercept
communications, and, so far as we are aware, the Minister has never taken any action to
follow up with the bureau why the inspector-general has raised these concerns in his last
report and what the Minister has done about it?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not able to answer that particular element of the
member’s question today, but what I would point out is that in response to the
Government Communications Security Bureau ra ising the issue, and the errors that it
has made, the Prime Minister moved very swif tly to act on these matters and called an
inquiry immediately, and that inquiry has reported today.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Is the Minister aware that in relation to the Government
Communications Security Bureau there is no standard parliamentary select committee
oversight, and the Official Information Act effectively cannot be applied, because the
bureau has a defence for not releasing the in formation under any circumstances, so the
sole democratic oversight for that organisa tion lies with the Minister responsible; and
does he believe that the Mini ster responsible is taking th at responsibili ty seriously
enough when we find out he does not know about the Kim Dotcom case, which started
in December?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think we are all very awar e of the unique nature of the
Government Communications Security Bureau agency. I think it is, indeed, indicative
of and underlines the Prime Minister’s view of his responsibility in this regard that
when the matter was brought to his attention he  immediately called an  inquiry into that
matter. He has advised the public, and the i nquiry has been reported. I would say that
that underlines how seriously he takes his role in this regard.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Given that for months the onl y person in authority in this
country who seemed not to know about Kim Dotcom was the Prime Minister—

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: Not true.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: It is true, for God’s sake—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would the member pl ease just ask his question.
[Interruption] No, order! The member will please ask his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, “Young Nick” keeps on shouting out. It is very—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member will just ask his question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I know he wants to get back into Cabinet. Given that for
months the only person in authority who did not know about Kim Dotcom or that plush
mansion just down the road from the Prime Mi nister’s electorate office was the Prime
Minister, why is he settling on a narro w inquiry into just the Government
Communications Security Bureau, when five other agencies all responsible in some way
to him never ever told him?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: All I can do is point out to  the member, who claimed he
had read the report from the inspector-gener al—but I now have my doubts, given his
question—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. We do not want
interpretation from that amateur. The fact is I have got two copies of the report—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member knows that is  totally outside the Standing
Orders and he is sk ating on thin ice. [ Interruption] Order! The member’s question was
not the most simple and direct question I have  ever heard in the H ouse and the Minister
is doing his best, I think, to answer it.
27 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5749

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I bow to the member’s obviou sly very, very long time in
the House, but my understanding of it is very  simple in relation to this matter: the
Government Communications Security Bureau  made two errors in relation to this
particular matter, and when it drew them to the Prime Minister’s attention, he
immediately called an inquiry. I am not quite  sure what the member is asserting the
Prime Minister should do in this regar d, but the bureau obvious ly made a serious
mistake, which is now being investigated.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: As I do not believe that the Government has tabled this report, I
seek leave to table the report from the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think that is publicly available right now. We will not bother with
that.
MediaWorks—Payment of Radio Broadcasting Licence Fees
5. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First)  to the Prime Minister: Did
MediaWorks have discussions with him in re lation to their application for a deferment
of their radio broadcasting licence fees; if so, what was the outcome?
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Economic Development)  on behalf of the

items.speaker: Prime Minister
items.text: The Prime Minister has had no formal  meetings with the board, senior
management, or representatives of MediaWor ks to discuss their radio broadcasting
licence fee. On one occasion in 2009 he ran into a Mr Brent Impey at a social event in
Auckland, where he briefly raised the issu e with the Prime Minister. He passed his
comments on to the responsible Minister.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Did one Steven Joyce present a paper to Cabinet on 12
October 2009 proposing the deferred payment sc heme, given that both the Ministry of
Economic Development and Treasury had advi sed that the Joyce scheme would expose
the Government to unnecessary financial risk? In short, why did the deal go ahead?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am sure the member is aware that Cabinet makes its
decisions on a weekly basis. I would point out that the matter he refers to was the
subject of a Government announcement on 22 October 2009.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. I asked whether the
Prime Minister was aware of one Steven Joyce presenting a Cabinet paper to Cabinet on
12 October 2009. Could we have an answer to that?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, well, sadly, the member did not  finish his question there. He
then asked: “Why did the proposal go ahead?”, and that is the bit the Minister answered.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, if that is the case he answered neither question, then.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Could I have an answer to at least one question?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! He answered the last part of the question. The member asked
why it went ahead and, if I heard the Minister  correctly, he said it was because Cabinet

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I put the rider on it:
given that both the Ministry of Economic  Development and Treasury had advised
against it, then why? We have had an answer to neither question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Well, forgive me; in my vi ew the Minister answered it. He
said it was because Cabinet decided—and Cabi nets often, in my experience, decide on
matters contrary to advice from all sorts of  departments—and that was the Minister’s
answer.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Has he received any reports regarding the financial trouble
of GR Media Holdings, the parent compa ny of MediaWorks, which recently posted a
$305 million loss; and is he concerned about  how this will impact on MediaWorks’
ability to pay back tens of millions of dollars of hard-earned taxpayers’ dollars?
5750 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, and I suggest that if he  wants the specifics in this
matter he might put the question down to the responsible Minister. But I am aware that
this particular payment is completely up to date.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, what responsibility does he intend to take—or what
responsibility does Steven Joyce intend to ta ke, as the Prime Minister extracted from
him—if this company goes belly up as the market says it is, and tens of millions of
dollars are lost to the New Zealand taxpayer, despite his mates’ rates arrangements?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I have tried to draw the member’s attention to the
Government announcement on 22 October 2009, and perhaps if I could quote a couple
of things from it in relation to the matter that the member raises. Firstly, it was made
clear that this is a commercial arrangement that was entered into at the time to allow the
whole radio industry some shor t-term flexibility of paym ent terms. Given the very
prominent, at that stage, global financial cr isis, it was available to all companies that
had renewals falling at the time of the height of the global financial crisis.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I seek leave to table a paper that sets out that the whole of
the industry, about which Mr Joyce speaks, is $300,000 to the rest of the industry and
the rest—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Could the member identify the document?

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Well, I will get it from the library shortly.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We do not—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I will get it from the library shortly. I have got time.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, we no longer seek leave to table documents that do not
exist.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I thought that the point the
Rt Hon Winston Peters was making was that  the document exists. I thought that under
the Standing Orders we had unt il the end of play to table documents that we could seek
leave—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We are not going to play around with the Standing Orders at
all. In this House it used to happen that leave was sought to table documents that did not
exist, and we are not going to have member s seeking leave to ta ble documents that do
not exist and then going to the library to try to assemble a document that might match
that.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. With respect, I have
seen the document—that is why I know the figures—but I have not got it with me. I
thought it would be in my papers today, and it is a bit remiss of me in not having it here.
All I am saying is I know the document exists. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! A point of order has been sought. As Speaker I must take the
member at his word. The member says he ha s seen this document, and therefore he is
telling the House that the doc ument exists. Leave is sought for the tabling of that
document. Is there any objection?

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: What is the document?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The document is a document from the library. The member needs to
be able to tell the House what the document is.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I am at liberty to say my research unit got the information I
believe, I am certain, from the library. That  is why I have got the figures already. I
mean, these are not hidden; they are known. The Government actually made the report
on the given day.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Now the member is debating. Seeking leave to table
documents is now a very precise operati on. I think we do not know enough about this
document for me to seriously seek leave from the House.
27 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5751
Oil, Gas, and Mineral Resources—Legislation and Initiatives
6. JONATHAN YOUNG (National—New Plymouth)  to the Minister of Energy
and Resources: What steps is the Government taking to encourage the development of
New Zealand’s oil, gas and mineral resources?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: Yesterday the Crown
Minerals (Permitting and Crown Land) Bill pass ed its first reading in this House. The
bill is a significant step in the Governme nt’s commitment to promote responsible
exploration and production of oil, gas, and mineral resources. The bill will also ensure
that the country receives a fair financial retu rn for those minerals so they can contribute
more to our economic development, as well as providing New Zealanders with greater
confidence in how the Government allocates rights to resources and how it is managing
and regulating those rights.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: What reports has the Minister seen on the potential of the oil, gas,
and minerals sector?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: I have seen a report from  the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment that shows that New Zealand is set to earn more than $3
billion in royalties from o ilfields and gasfields already in production. If patterns of
exploration and development increase, future royalty income could generate up to $12.7
billion for New Zealand. This is new money that can be in vested in schools, hospitals,
and roads. This is why the Government wants to realise the economic benefits from
developing our oil, gas, and mineral resources in a safe and environmentally responsible
manner.

items.speaker: Jonathan Young
items.text: What other work is the Govern ment progressing in relation to
ensuring a strong regulatory regime for oil and gas exploration?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: The Government recently passed new environmental
legislation that will allow us to carefully  manage development in an environmentally
responsible way of our enormous resources that lie in our oceans. We also recently
reviewed New Zealand’s marine oil spil l preparedness and response capability. The
Government is also currently reviewing the health and safety regulations that apply to
petroleum operations and is reviewing the minimum insurance requirements for
offshore installations. I wait with interest for the Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment’s investigation into hydraulic fracturing. So, as you can see, there are
several reforms going on at the moment that w ill ensure that we have a more robust but
progressive regulatory regime.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Kia ora t ātou. Does the Minister agre e with the submission of
Ngati Porou, in response to the review of the Crown Minerals Ac t that preceded the
legislation he mentioned ea rlier, that “the Crown is  proposing what Ngati Porou
considers to be the progressive removal and/ or softening of environmental protections
and the already limited protections available to iwi.”; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL HEATLEY
items.text: No. The Crown’s obligations to  iwi and to the environment
are already significant. Processes for disc harging those obligations are established
through the minerals programmes. Those oblig ations and principles set out in the
minerals programmes are sound and broad en ough to take care of what the member
raises.
Jobs—Statistics
7. Hon DAVID PARKER (Labour)  to the Minister of Finance: Does he stand by
his statement “the Government is doing ev erything it can to give businesses the
confidence to invest, grow and create new jobs”; if so, what was the net change in filled
jobs in the private sector from December 2008 to December 2011 according to Statistics
New Zealand’s Quarterly Employment Survey?
5752 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister
of Finance : Yes, the Minister does stand by that  statement. The official measure of
employment and unemployment, which is the household labour force survey, shows that
57,000 more New Zealanders are in a job no w than 2 years ago. In contrast, the
quarterly employment survey, which the memb er raises, has a number of gaps. It does
not include agriculture, for example, which is reasonably significant in the New Zealand
context, or the self-employed, which is al so significant, and it excludes around half a
million jobs in the economy. With that in mind, over the period the member has
selected, that survey reports that the numbe r of filled jobs fell by 30,000, but it is also
important to note that that loss happened in just one single quarter at the height of the
recession, and then there was the global financial crisis.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Why does he prefer the measur e of the household labour force
survey, when just about everyone other than him knows that it counts someone who has
three jobs, each of which could be just an  hour long, as three more people employed in
New Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Actually, the member’s changing choice of documents is
quite amusing. It is interesting to note, though,  that the reason we choose it is that it is
the official measure, but do not take our word for it. Between 1999 and 2008 the
number of press releases issued by the previous Government that mentioned the
household labour force survey was 78. The number that mentioned the quarterly
employment survey, which the member refers to today, was two. So I think the previous
Government was in favour of the household labour force survey, as well.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given his preference for the hous ehold labour force survey and
given that it now shows there are 162,000 people unemployed as of June 2012, does it
concern him that on that measure there are more unemployed New Zealanders now than
at any other point under this Government?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure about the veraci ty of the last statement that
the member made in that question, but what I can say to him is, obviously—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. A member is not allowed
to question another member’s veracity. The member made a statement in this House. He
can say he does not agree with it, but he cannot question his veracity.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: To disagree with “the veracity of it” I think is getting too precious
altogether. I have never known the honourable me mber himself to be quite so precious,
to be fair.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: As I said, I am not sure about that last statement that the
member has raised, but I can say that of cour se the Government is very keen to have
more New Zealanders employed. We are actually doing pretty well relative to the rest of
the world. I appreciate that we are not doi ng well compared with “Planet Labour”, but
we have had, of course, the global financ ial crisis, we have had the Canterbury
earthquakes, and, actually, we are making good progress. And I note that in the business
confidence survey released today, some thing like 26 percent of businesses were
expecting an increase in activity over the ne xt 12 months, and that is very encouraging
for jobs in this country.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I seek leave to table a document prepared by the Parliamentary
Library showing that accordi ng to the household labour for ce survey unemployment is
now 162,000, and that it is the highest it has been under this Government.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Could the Minister please remind the House what is the official
measure of unemployment?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question actually should be, I guess, “What is the official
measure of unemployment?”. What the memb er said was not actu ally a question. I
invite him to actually pose it as a question.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What is the official measure of unemployment?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The official measure of unemployment and employment is
the household labour force survey, which shows some 57,000 more New Zealanders are
in a job now than there were 2 years ago. That is a good-news story for New Zealand.
As I said to the House before, the further good news is that business confidence in terms
of own expectations is growing very signi ficantly. Actually we are coming out of the
global financial crisis, which I know did not occur on “Planet Labour”, very well.

items.text: If he came to this House prep ared to say that the official
measure of employment and unemployment is the household labour force survey, why
could he not answer my question, which asked him directly whether it was now
showing unemployment at 162,000, and confirm that that is the highest it has been

items.text: The point is that I acknowledged in the answer that it is
higher than we all would like—I think everybody in this House—but the Government is

items.text: Does he still stand by the promise made during the 2011

National Certificate of Educational Achievement—2011 Results
10. SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki) to the Minister of Education :
What reports has she received on the 2011 NCEA results?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I have received the final report on
2011 school-leaver qualification data for National Certificate of Educational
Achievement (NCEA) results, and I am deli ghted, as I am sure all members of the
House will be, with the improvements across the board. Last year nearly 72 percent of
all school-leavers attained at least NCEA level 2, compared with 69 percent in 2010 and
66 percent in 2009. That is up 6 percent in the last 3 years. I am delighted with this
result and I know we can do better, and I look forward to further increases next year and
in future years.
Simon O’Connor: What does the 2011 NCEA level 2 data show about the outcomes
for Māori and Pasifika school-leavers?

items.speaker: Hon HEKIA PARATA
items.text: I am happy to say that the data shows we are already
making a significant impact on the number of young M āori leaving school with NCEA
level 2. Last year 51 percent of M āori students left school w ith NCEA level 2, up from
44 percent in 2009 and 48 percent in 2010. That is up 7 percent in the last 3 years.
Similarly, 63 percent of Pasifika students le ft with NCEA level 2, compared with 59
27 Sep 2012 Questions for Oral Answer 5755
percent in 2010 and 56 pe rcent in 2009. That is up another 7 percent in the last 3 years.
Although this is a very good result and shows we are on the right track, our Government
has much higher aspirations for our young pe ople. We think we can do much better,
with a clear focus on lifting achievement for five out of five learners.

11. JAN LOGIE (Green)  to the Minister of Justice : Will she give full

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: Can she confirm that the alternative trial processes report is no longer on
the Law Commission’s work programme and is on hold indefinitely, despite
submissions being called for only 7 months  ago and there having been decades of
research showing that change is urgently n eeded to protect sexual abuse victims in our
courts?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I can confirm that the Law Commission has a great body
of work that it is working th rough. This report is not the hi ghest priority that it has. I
would have to say to the member that I shar e her concerns for, particularly, the victims
of violent sexual abuse. However, we cannot  have a system where there is a civil
system, or one particular system, for those victims and those who are accused, and then
a completely different system for someone who is accused of another terrible violent
crime such as murder or kidnapping.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
items.text: If she shares my concerns, why is this work programme on hold
indefinitely, despite only 13 percent of sexual violence cases result ing in a conviction
and one in five complainants backing out before the case is over?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: Well, of course I share the concerns that the member has
for victims of crime. However, that does not  mean that we should victimise others by
way of having one particular trial process for one strand of offences, and completely
different trial processes for other strands. I know  that there has been quite a lot of work
that has been done from various quarters on th is, but at the end of the day we have a
system where we have a common law system, and there is work that is being done and
has been done, particularly around child witnes ses. That work is ongoing. It is currently
with parliamentary counsel for drafting. But this is not something where I believe we
could have—and I could note some of the comments that Mr Charles Chauvel has made
on this very issue, when he has said, and certainly the Labour me mbers have said, on
the Victims of Crime Reform Bill: “We are mindful of the wisdom of warnings from the
Chief Justice and others that any change”—

items.speaker: Charles Chauvel
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am delighted that the

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think there is no need to be quoting. The Minister is not
responsible for what Mr Chauvel may have said.

items.speaker: Jan Logie
