items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: New Zealand First is calling for a commission
of inquiry as our leader, the Rt Hon Winston Peters, has already said in the House this
afternoon. We have heard of so much bungling on behalf of so many agencies in this
country in the last 9 or 10 months over this Dotcom saga —including right to the top,
including the bungling of the Prime Minister, and includin g the incompetent handling
by the Prime Minister—that this needs an independent commission of inquiry.
Let us go back to the very beginning—let  us go back to the very beginning. The
Ōrewa community constable, Jason Homan, vi sited the Dotcom mansion the day before
the raid. He knocked on the front door. He  was welcomed in by Mr Dotcom. He was
given a tour around the building,  and they discussed Mr Dotcom’s security. He wanted
to assist Mr Dotcom with his security. Bu t what he did not let on was that he had a
covert camera hidden on his body, and the wh ole time this community constable, who
was supposedly there in Mr Dotcom’s intere st, was actually filming in preparedness for
the raid the next morning. The following morning at dawn helicopters start dropping out
of the sky and 80 members of the Special Tactics Group of the New Zealand Police
come off these helicopters—80 of them—and al so via cars and othe r things coming up
the roads, and they force entry into the mansion. They drag Mr Dotcom’s 27-weeks
pregnant wife out on to the lawn in the rain  at dawn. They terrorise the children in the
house. They then find Mr Dotcom and drag him outside as well, and he is pushed down
onto the ground where he sustains  some injuries to some of his limbs that were stood
on. There were police, supposedly, in this raid wearing T-shirts, jeans, and flak jackets,
which is most unusual for the New Zealand Police, and there is speculation that some of
those may well have been members of agenci es from abroad, including the FBI—there
is speculation on that.
This is the sort of thing going on in this country within a relatively short distance and
in the Prime Minister’s own electorate of Helensville.
5770 Urgent Debates 27 Sep 2012
In the Prime Minister’s own electorate of Helensville—in his own electorate—this is
all going on, while he is the Minister res ponsible for the GCSB—the spy organisation
for this country. In his own electorate, this sort of thing is going on. That very same spy
organisation did not even real ise that this individual was living in the most expensive
mansion in the Prime Minister’s electorate, worth $30 million, with 50 staff. How many
houses in New Zealand have 50 staff? Not many. Maybe the Prime Minister has quite a
few; he is probably the second in the country with staff. But for the mansion to be in his
own electorate and not now admit to the fact that he knew of Dotcom , that people from
Dotcom’s staff had been to his electorate o ffice, that there had been numerous dialogue
with his office about it, and for this Prime Mi nister to say that he  really knew about all
the intricacies of the details of this only in  the last week or so, is balderdash—absolute
balderdash. This is a cover-up—an absolute  cover-up. The fact that the Deputy Prime
Minister, as Acting Prime Minister, back  on 16 August signed a warrant—while the
Prime Minister was away at his baseball ga me in the United States—to provide for a
cover-up to bury all the details is even more of an indictment on this Prime Minister that
this is an absolute whitewash.
New Zealanders expect more of any Government—any Government—and in this
particular case the Prime Minister himself should be standing down, stepping aside, and
calling for a commission of inquiry. Any other Minister who was this incompetent in
handling his portfolio would have been st ood down while there was an inquiry. He
should stand by the same measur es, stand by the same standa rds, step aside, and let
people come in and do a proper job. He s hould spend less time on the golf course, less
time in his holiday house in Hawaii, and less time on the global stage getting
photographs with everybody he can possibl y get his hands on, and spend more time
overlooking his own portfolios. New Zealand First calls for a commission of inquiry.
Let us get on with it.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I note that the Prime Minister
has this afternoon apologised to Kim Dotcom for the basic errors of his agency. What
he has not apologised for is wh at is really the co re of this debate, and that is his
slackness in his oversight of that agency.
I would like to give many members of the H ouse a little bit of a history lesson going
back to 1977, when I had a notable appearance in  this House, and was, in fact, arrested
during debate on the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service Amendment Bill. The
reason that I was arrested then was that I be lieved that there was too much power being
centralised in the hands of one person—at that stage it was Sir Robert Muldoon—and I
did not believe that there were systems ar ound them to ensure that there was proper
supervision of the Prime Minister.
Since that time there have been some changes made that have improved the
legislation slightly, but, more  important, ever since that  time there have been Prime
Ministers who have treated their role in  this area diligently. They have worked
diligently. They have been briefed. They have read their papers. They have asked the
questions that needed to be asked. I can re member one occasion when I was with Helen
Clark in her car, early in her prime ministerial time, and both the driver and I got booted
out of her car. She borrowed my phone, b ecause I had a Vodafone phone that was
properly secure and she only had a Telecom phone, so that she could be properly briefed
on an urgent matter. It was so important that she did not want to wait for half an hour to
get to a secure landline; she wanted to do that.
The question I have got is whether this Prim e Minister interests hi mself at all in the
work of his security agencies, or is he pr epared to say “OK, boys, just go and do what
you want. OK, boys, just go and do what you wa nt. I’m not going to ask, because if I
ask, I might know. And if I know that you’re  doing something wrong, I’ll be in even
27 Sep 2012 Urgent Debates 5771
worse trouble.”? That is what the situation is here. The Prime Minister was not prepared
to apologise to this House for what he kne w happened. He was not prepared to go into
the detail in Parliament, the place where he is meant to be held accountable. He runs
away. He does not front up. He does not front  up in this House a nd apologise for the
fact that he is not doing his job properly. He is meant to uphold ministerial standards.
That is his job. He is the Prime Minister. He is meant to be above all others.
And, in this case, his plea of  ignorance is just not good enough. Ignorance is not an
excuse when you are the Prime Minister who is  meant to be superv ising an agency, an
agency where the relationship is much clos er, and the supervision necessarily much
closer, than, for example, with the police or  any other Government agency. This stuff
very rarely gets anywhere near  a court. There is very rare ly a check or a balance on the
power of the Prime Minister and these ag encies. Our entire democracy depends on his
agency doing its job properly, and for that to happen the Prime Minister must supervise
it. To say that he cannot know anything about th e operations is just horse shit. It is just
absolute nonsense. The Prime Minister mu st know about the areas where there are
operations going on. The Prime Minister has to know that there are matters that he
should be looking at.
We have given this Prime Minister a lot of support in this area. There is an enormous
amount of trust that goes to every—

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: Better than that.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: I agree with that member there. The Prime Minister
should be better than that. I agree with that member. Every other Prime Minister going
right back in my entire time in Parliament ha s been better than that. Which member is
that?

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: I’m not sure.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: The one with glasses, next to—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Scott Simpson.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: It was Scott Simpson, I am told. Scott Simpson says
we deserve better than that, a nd I totally agree with him. We deserve a Prime Minister
who reads his documents, a Prime Minister who gets briefed. What we have seen here is
a debacle, an absolute failure of a Prime Minister to run a spy agency with integrity. It is
his job to run it with integrit y. It is his job to look careful ly at what it is doing, because
he is the democratic check on the system. A nd when he does not do his job properly, as
he clearly has not done now, then the democra tic check that should be there is absent.
The agency runs amuck, it breaks the law, and it spies on people it is not meant to be
spying on.
There is another question. There is another question that needs to be asked. We know
that the information has been flowing. We know  that the assistance has been flowing to
the United States. Is it correct —is it correct—that US agencies were also involved in
covert surveillance within New Zeala nd, with the full knowledge of the Prime
Minister’s agency? Did a foreign agency act contrary to New Zealand law? Did a
foreign agency act contrary to New Zealand law, with the connivance of an agency for
which the Prime Minister is responsible? If that is the case, then I expect that any Prime
Minister with integrity will be a position where they cannot survive—where they cannot
survive—because it is the role of the Prime Minister to make sure  that these “boy’s
own” tricks do not occur. It is his job to ma ke sure that the spies do not run amuck.
They have an enormous amount of power, and if the suggestio n is that overseas
agencies—as well as our own Government  Communications Security Bureau—were
acting covertly in New Zealand, with the co nnivance, with the assistance, with the
knowledge of our security agenci es, if that was occurring, then  that is even worse than
what has occurred here.
5772 Urgent Debates 27 Sep 2012
The other question that we still have not heard any confirmation of is whether, as
was alleged in the Dominion Post this morning, the immigration file for Kim Dotcom
was, in fact, given to th e police before the raid—w ell before the raid—by the
Immigration Service. It is a pretty basic que stion: was it given or was it not given? And
if it was given—the Immigra tion Service says that it wa s—what we want to know is
whether anyone bothered to read it. Did an yone bother reading the file that was
supplied? Did Maurice Williamson? Maurice is here. Maurice knows a bit about land
information, and that sort of area. Jonathan Coleman knows a bit about that area. Simon
Power knows a bit about that ar ea. I will just tell  you what used to happen. In the old
Government, if two Ministers disagreed and one overruled the other, then you made a
file note and the Prime Minister had a look. When you had a difference, when you had a
Minister overruling another Minister and it was something that was important to the
Government, you wrote it down. You wrot e it down. Maurice Williamson is nodding.
You know what I think happened? I think the Pr ime Minister did not read it. I think the
Prime Minister did not read it. Well, he did not read the police report, wilfully—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member, but his time has expired.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I want to just to uch on a couple of the
comments made by the previous speaker, Mr Mallard, and, in particular, his claim that
the Prime Minister was not prepared to front up. I think this is something that needs to
be addressed, because what the member is inferring is that the Prime Minister should
act—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I cannot “infer” anything
in my speech. I think you mean “imply”.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I infer from those things that the member feels that
the Prime Minister should have  taken action before all the f acts were before him, and,
indeed, he called for an apology. But the prude nt thing to do was to  conduct an inquiry,
and to need to have the inquiry  to establish all the facts. The facts are now on the table.
The Prime Minister has apologised to Mr Kim Dotcom and has expressed his
disappointment in the events that have transpired.
But I also think it quite rich for Mr Mallard to say that the Prime Minister should
take control of these agencies, because Ministers—as that member well knows—do not
run agencies. In fact, I well recall responses to oral questions in this House when Mr
Mallard was the Associate Minister of Transport, and calls fo r him to take control of an
issue related to Air New Zealand and th e Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing
Union in respect of a maintenance dispute at Christchurch Airport. He was at very great
pains to point out that it was absolutely not a Minister’s role to interfere with the day-to-
day running of Government agencies—so I sense, at least, an inconsistency—or, for that
matter, a State-owned enterprise like Air New Zealand, which would have been even
worse, frankly. So the member says one th ing in Government, and another thing in
Opposition.
But it is clear, and, indeed, the lawyers act ing for Mr Dotcom ha ve indicated, that
information contained in the report that was released today could be used as evidence in
the extradition hearing that is currently be fore the High Court. As such, it would be
entirely inappropriate for any member of the Government—or this House, frankly—to
comment on the matters that may yet be before the court. There are very strict protocols
in respect of the legislatur e’s boundaries in respect of judicial proceedings—and vice
versa, I should add—and I think Minister Fi nlayson very clearly explained the reasons
why and the aspects of the report. I just  want to endorse those comments by the
Attorney-General and say no more about it.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5773
NATIONAL WAR MEMORIAL PARK (PUKEAHU) EMPOWERING BILL
Third Reading

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.role: Minist er for Arts, Culture and Heritage

items.text: I move, That the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill be now read
a third time . I am very pleased to have played my part in steering this National War
Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill through the House. I certainly acknowledge
and appreciate the support that has been re ceived from all parties, with the obvious
exceptions of the Greens and the Mana party.

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: Disappointing.

items.speaker: Hon CHRISTOPHER FINLAYSON
items.text: I am disappointed, but not surprised, by their
attitude. I think what they fail to appreciate is  that since I became the Minister for Arts,
Culture and Heritage in 2008 a lot of work has gone into this project to ensure that the
cut-and-cover option became a reality. It is  simply and plainly wrong to say—as, I
think, Holly Walker said at the Committee st age—that the plans have been around for
some years. I think Mr Chauvel may have made a similar allegation in his rather
peculiar contribution in the first reading debate. They are both plain wrong. The 2008
plans provided for State Highway  1 to go through the park. I wa s first alerted to that by
Deputy Mayor Ian McKinnon in 2008. I spoke to Mt Cook School and said that I
thought that was really most unfortunate. I ha ve worked since then to see if we could
get this result, and we have.
We have the bill. The bill was introduced. It was referred to the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee on 28 August. Th at committee worked very hard, and I
salute its chair and members, because it reported the bill back to the House on 18
September. I also want to acknowledge the contributions from the submitters and the
officials from both the New Zealand Transpor t Agency and my ministry, the Ministry
for Culture and Heritage, who have worked very hard on this matter.
This legislation is required to complete the memorial in time for the centenary of the
Gallipoli landings, and this very speedy prog ression will enable Government agencies
to start work in October on what will be New Zealand’s major legacy project for the

items.speaker: First World War commemorations
items.text: this wonderf ul park, Pukeahu. It is the centrepiece
of the Government’s programme of projects and activities to mark the centenary over
the 2014-18 period. The joint agency WW100 Programme Office in the Ministry for
Culture and Heritage is going to lead a nd facilitate commemorative activities in
accordance with other organisations of the Crown like the New Zealand Defence Force,
the Department of Internal Affairs, the Mi nistry of Foreign A ffairs and Trade, and
others, and a panel of trusted New Zealande rs is going to be guiding and informing
these activities. During this period the war memorial is very much going to be a focus of
the First World War commemorations and also , increasingly, of a number of significant
70th anniversaries of the Second World War and, as time progresses, of anniversaries for
both the Viet Nam and Korean wars. This bill is going to ensure that we have a park that
provides a more appropriate setting for these very important commemorative activities.
What the bill does is it grants resource consents, heritage authorisations, and
building consents, and provides for the desi gnation of the land, and powers of entry on
to the land. It grants rights to the Mini stry for Culture and Heritage and the New
Zealand Transport Agency to complete th e undergrounding of State Highway 1 and the
memorial park in time for the centenary of the Gallipoli landings in April 2015. In
doing so, what it is going to do is remove th e standard objection and appeal rights
available under the Resource Management Act 1991, the Historic Places Act 1993, and
the Public Works Act 1981, but I emphasise th at rights to compensation under the latter
Act are going to be preserved. And should the n eed arise, the bill will also enable the
5774 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
Governor-General to issue Orders in Counc il to grant further c onsents than those
covered in the schedules of the bill.
But it is extremely important to note that there are safeguards to provide oversight of
these Orders in Council, and a review pa nel is going to be c onvened to scrutinise
recommendations for those Orders in Council. That panel will report to the Minister at
6-monthly intervals, and the Minister will provide a copy of that report to the House.
Parliament is also going to have the power to disallow an Order in Council within 12
sitting days after the day on which it was presented to the House. So what has happened
here is that every step has been taken to ensu re that the focus and the purpose of the bill
are tightly defined, to avoid any risk that powers may be used for anything other than
the intended national purpose. The bill also ensures continuing input from important
stakeholders like Mt Cook School, the Wellington City Council, the Wellington Tenths
Trust, the Port Nicholson Block Settlement Trust, and other organisations representing
local residents and road users.
Like many public memorials, the developm ent of this National War Memorial has
proceeded in fits and starts. In the 1920s there was a debate over what form it should
take. There was some talk that there coul d even be a memorial parade or a new
cathedral, and then a Wellingt on jeweller, Mr Denton, suggested the Carillon with bells
of remembrance, and that was the idea th at was enthusiastically embraced by the
community. The Wellington War Memorial Cari llon Society raised the money for a 49-
bell carillon and presented the funds to the Government. The Government then made its
contribution towards the construc tion of the bell towers to house the Carillon. Gummer
and Ford were two persons who won the design competition for the bell tower and the
new national museum behind it. Gummer was renowned for his work on memorials. I
think he was responsible for the Massey Me morial on Watts Peninsula and the Bridge
of Remembrance in Christchurch. And so it wa s in 1932 that the publ ic flocked to this
new memorial. At last, New Zealanders had a surrogate tomb for the thousands who
had, sadly, died overseas in service of their country.
The next stage was supposed to be an  adjoining Hall of Memories, but its
construction was cut short be cause of the Depression and then the Second World War.
Indeed, it was to be 32 years before that building was finally opened in 1964. In 2004
Kingsley Baird’s Tomb of the Unknown Wa rrior was added to the complex, and the
remains of an unnamed soldier from Caterp illar Valley Cemetery near Longueval were
interred in the tomb.
I give the House that history because it is im portant to recognise that this has been a
developing project, but with this developmen t we will be able to say that we finally
have a complete memorial to those who have  served this country so well. With the
completion of the project, the impressive ar chitecture of the memorial is going to be
complemented by a park of equivalent  substance and design. The National War
Memorial and the various elements of the pr ecinct will be unified. It is going to be a
place of quiet reflection where people can congregate for important national
commemorations, and our allies will also be  honoured with their own memorials. I
emphasise that there is also going to be an interpretation centre, where young New
Zealanders who attend Anzac Day commemorations will be able to learn more about the
tumultuous events that have left their mark  on this country. So too will visitors to
Wellington from around the country and overseas be drawn to the memorial.
In the future, I believe the pr ecinct is most likely to be included in the Government’s
proposed national historic landm ark list of places that are significant national treasures
to New Zealand. Last but not least, the tr affic noise is going to be greatly reduced
because this tunnelling is to take place. Ever yone is delighted that this is going to
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5775
proceed. To have had State Highway 1 trav ersing a sacred memorial, frankly, would
have been inappropriate and, indeed, disrespectful.
There is keen interest in the developm ent. I am looking forward to attending
community meetings to talk to people about it. I am very keen to keep in touch with
people. I think this is going to be a memori al of which we are going to be very proud
indeed.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and
speak in this third reading debate on th e National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu)
Empowering Bill. The Minister for Arts, Cu lture and Heritage, who has just spoken,
gave us an interesting history lesson around act ivities in the park and the war memorial.
He could not bring himself to say the words “Helen Clark”. It is unfortunate that the
Minister, whom, I think, we have given some  credit to that he has been a person who
has worked on this issue over the last few y ears—he has stuttered al ong a little bit, but
now we have finally got there—could not manage to say that in 2004 Helen Clark put
forward this idea. The words could not leave his mouth, which is a pity because this is
something that people on both sides of the House have certainly wanted.
I want to make just a few points here. The fi rst thing I want to do is just to thank the
officials who worked on this particular bill. This bill was dealt with at speed, at pace. A
lot of pressure was placed on officials to be ab le to not only come up with the bill in the
first place but also then deal with the submissions. A number of significant changes
were made during the select committee proce ss, and they had to be made at pace. The
officials from the New Zealand Transport Agency, the Ministry for Culture and
Heritage, and also the Parliamentary Counsel Office did do a terrific job in getting that
work done. I think in a piece of legislation like this that should be recognised.
This memorial park will be a place that will become integral, I believe, to New
Zealand’s heritage and history. It will be a place where New Zealanders can reflect on
the sacrifice of those who have gone to war and also on the cost of war. It will also be a
place where we will be able to highlight our relationship with countries such as
Australia, which has offered to put a memori al within the park. I was very heartened
that at the first of the community meetings  we had on this, Minister Chris Finlayson
said that he would be looking to see within the park some  kind of memorial to those
who were conscientious objector s to war. He mentioned at that meeting, in particular,
Archibald Baxter. I think that is a very appropriate thing fo r this park. It should be a
place of reflection. It should be a place wher e people can go to think about the overall
impact of war. I was very heartened that Mr  Finlayson had said that. I certainly support
that idea.
It is, obviously, timed to be ab le to be open in 2015 on the 100 th commemorations of
the Gallipoli landings. The year 2015 will be a very important time for New Zealanders
in terms of our sense of identity and looking back over our history as  a country. This is
a great legacy project for that time. It would be better if we could have gone through the
correct legislative processes, regulatory pr ocesses, and consenting processes that would
be required for that, but time is against us. On this side of the House we look warily at
empowering-type legislation, but in this ca se this is such a nationally significant
project—a project that does need, for symbolic reasons, to be able to be there in April
2015—that we can agree to this legislation. But we make clear on this side of the House
that it is not a habit that we want to see in this House, to have empowering legislation
that does override objection and appeal rights . That is not something this House should
do regularly, and we certainly will not support it to be done regularly.
What we have done in this legislation is  attempt to put in place measures that
mitigate the fact that we ar e doing empowering legislation. The Minister has mentioned
the review panel that will look at any Orde rs in Council that are being asked for by the
5776 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
Minister, and that review pane l, in turn, has to report to this Parliament on a 6-monthly
basis, so that this Parliament has some role. I think those are important provisions in this
law. I think what is particularly important and which was added at the Transport and
Industrial Relations Committee is  clause 24(4), which is what  we call the last resort
provision. This is to make absolutely clear th at the use of Orders in Council should be a
last resort. The phrase is that  the Minister must have cons idered “all other reasonably
practicable ways relevant” to this legislation to achieve the goals that the Order in
Council is trying to achieve. That is a stat ement to a Minister that they must have
considered all other matters. We know that  an Order in Council, which, as we know,
takes away the rights of this Parliament, can be used only as a la st resort under this
legislation. That is a significant clause, a nd I am very pleased that the Government
agreed to the inclusion of it in this bill.
Beyond the question of the Orders in Council, I want to speak about the role of the
community in this project. The community forum that is being set up with this bill is an
excellent process. The addition the select co mmittee made was to include the idea that
the local community could have a role in th e final design of this park, and I hope the
Government takes that seriously. The final de sign of this park will mean a lot to the
people of the Mount Cook community and th e wider Wellington community, and it is
important that the Government listens to those communities. There are concerns already
being raised by those who are perhaps involved  in one part in particular, the historic
creche that is just on the fringes of the park. They will be impacted on by this. I urge the
Government to talk to the community, to listen to the community, and to use that
community forum, not just the three times a ye ar that it is possible to use it but more
often, to ensure that the community is invol ved. I also urge the Government to ensure
that the residents of Wellingt on, not just those in my electorate in Wellington Central
but more broadly across the city, are kept info rmed about this project. It will start very,
very soon, and people in Wellington may not be aware of the disruption that is coming
their way.
I want to make reference to a couple of gr oups that I think it is very important are
considered here. The first of those is th e Wellington City Council. The Wellington City
Council has generously offered $5 million for th is project. It is a key stakeholder. It
must be involved all the wa y through this project. Ho pefully, working with the
Wellington City Council, we can see the deve lopment of this park, this great green
space for Wellington, integrated within ot her plans that the Wellington City Council
has. I thank the council for its support for this project. I part icularly want to
acknowledge the work of Deputy Mayor Ia n McKinnon and also Mayor Celia Wade-
Brown, who have been strong supporters of this project.
The other organisations I want to mention are the Taranaki Wh ānui and the Port
Nicholson Block Settlement Trust. They ar e landowners within th e park area. They
have a long historical associati on with this area. Their name for this area forms part of
this bill. Their rights to be spoken to and talked to are important, and I am disappointed
that we were not able to perhaps find the accommodation within the bill that they
wanted. But they can rest assured that through the schedules of this bill and the
community forum, the Taranaki Whānui and the Port Nicholson Block Settlement Trust
are acknowledged for their important role and w ill be a key part of the development of
the park.
The last group that I want to mention in this context is the local community, and the
fact that in this bill we have added in to the community forum and the consultation
processes around traffic plans and the future place of buildings in the park the owners of
the Mount Cook Police Barracks and the Ta sman Garden Body Corporate, the two
buildings that sit either side of Tasman St reet and the intersection with Buckle Street.
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5777
They are representative of the interests of the local community, as is the local residents
association, Mount Cook Mobi lised, which has also done a fantastic job of advocating
for this park. It wants this park. It will become a vital part of the Mount Cook
community. The Mt Cook School, with its terr ific principal, Sandy McCallum, is also
part of that. This is something that it will  be uniquely associated with, and it is vitally
important that in the development of the park it is a key stakeholder as well.
Overall, the Labour Party is happy to support this legislation. It is  not ideal that we
are passing empowering legislation, but this  reaches the threshold of a nationally
significant project. I know that veterans, th eir families, and all those affected by war
will know that this is an important thing. But, much beyond that, for Wellingtonians this
will be a terrific place of reflection, a gr een space, and an open place for people to
spend time. It will also attract visitors, I predict, from not only New Zealand but right
across the world. It will be something that  we can be proud of and that will pay
appropriate tribute to the sacr ifice of those who have gone to war and to the costs of
war. I support this bill.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: I wish to take a call and
support in essence the previous two speeches  from Minister Finlayson and also the
deputy leader of the Labour Party, Grant Robe rtson, who was there on the day that this
project was launched with the Prime Minister and with the Mayor and Deputy Mayor of
Wellington City. We know that this project is hugely signi ficant. I was there yesterday
with the Prime Minister, the Minister of De fence, and Iain Lees -Galloway representing
the Opposition, when we were commemorating the 70 th anniversary celebrations of the
Bomber Command. Of course, 32 of those vete rans travelled to London and were back
sharing their experiences yesterday at the National War Memorial and also at a function
in the Grand Hall afterwards.
It was interesting standing down on the edge  of State Highway 1 on Buckle Street,
waiting to greet the Prime Minister, with all of that traffic zooming by. When the Prime
Minister did arrive, meeting other representatives, the noise of State Highway 1 was not
something that was desirable for the National War Memorial Park, which we want to
establish there. So thank goodness that the Prime Minister has stepped up to the plate
and sought some extra funding to ensure that we can cut and cover the project, so that
State Highway 1 can be underground. When we  get to the special significance of the
centennial of those 2,721 who lost their lives  at Gallipoli, almost 100 years ago—it will
be in 2015, when the park is open—we can stand there and celebrate in essence what
they did for our country.
On that note, I think it is important for everyone to realise that we are in a space
where we have an online survey seeking s upport from New Zealanders and interest
from those who want to travel to Gallipo li in 2015. We are seeking their feedback and
we have an online survey that is open until 25 Novemb er. I urge those who are
interested to get involved and give us thei r feedback. Early indications are that there
will be 30,000 or 40,000 New Zealanders who want to travel to Gallipoli in 2015.
For those in the House who ha ve been on the peninsula, and I was fortunate to go
this year, we all realise that it is pretty much a national park, that the Turkish authorities
have to be involved in managing the numbers, and that means that there will be a ballot
process similar to what there has been for the Olympics, the recent royal wedding, etc.,
etc. We are going to have to manage the ex pectations, and the indi cations are that we
will be allocated somewhere in the vicinity  of 2,000 places, and that is lining up with
Australia, which will be allocated somewher e in the vicinity of 8,000 places. It is in
essence going to be sorted by the proportion of  fatalities that we lo st on the Gallipoli
Peninsula.
5778 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
In conclusion, this is a very important project. I acknowledge all of the people who
have been involved in this project to get it to where it is now. I am sure the whole of the
House is going to be really excited that, come 2015, we are go ing to have a very special
place to commemorate and say thank you to al l the veterans who have served for New
Zealand. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: As you have already heard in this
House, Labour supports the National War Me morial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill,
and now we are in the final stages of its  passage. It will be welcomed by many, many
New Zealanders, veterans and the community—particularly the local community here in
Wellington. This bill has had strong local support, not only from those who live in the
direct vicinity but also from around Wellington in general and also, I think, from around
New Zealand, from those wanting to have a place that we could call a National War
Memorial Park.
This bill will enable the completion of the park by 2015 to commemorate the 100 th
anniversary of Gallipoli. But, as the Minister for Arts, Cultu re and Heritage said in his
third reading speech, it will also be a place where we can commemorate other conflicts
that New Zealand has been involved in. There are a number coming up of 70 th
anniversary commemorations.
One of those that it would have been nice to be able to commemorate, had the park
been built earlier, was the battle for Crete. I was fortunate to represent our country at the
65th anniversary of the Battle of Crete. It  was a most moving occasion, but very few
people could actually go to Crete to commem orate that battle. Most New Zealanders
will never be able to go there, so I was pr ivileged. Being able to go to a place like the
National War Memorial and being able to co mmemorate events with others who were
there, and their families and their grandchildren, I think will be a really significant part
of this new park.
It is a little bit like going to the Atat ürk Memorial. The Minister in his speech—in
fact, actually, no. It was not the Minister in his speech; it was something that Helen
Clark said at the time that she proposed this park. She said it would be a place where
other countries could have memorials and be  able to commemorate events when they
had been in partnership in war with New Z ealand. That is why I mentioned the Atatürk
Memorial in my electorate. If you have not been there on Anzac Day, I suggest that you
do so. It is the most moving service that you can go to. It is a relationship between
Turkey and New Zealand. I am told that the spot where it has been  built is very like
Anzac Cove, and it has a very spiritual feeling about it. Th is new National War
Memorial Park will mean that other countries will be able to put up memorials as well.
This bill was not without some debate as to the process that would be used for the
establishment of this park, because it does remove appeals under a number of Acts, and
there is the use of Orders in Council. I understand concerns that members have about
the use of Orders in Council and proper proces s, but I said in my speeches that it would
have been really good if we had comple te agreement across this House for the
establishment of this park. Unfortunately, th e Greens have decided to oppose it, and to
me that is a little bit like having a bob each way. They were in favour of it, but they
opposed it, where, on this occasion, for some thing as significant as this that was not
going to cause a huge problem because there is so much community support for it, it
would be good if we had unanimous support acro ss Parliament. Maybe, even at this late
stage, the Greens might like to consider supporting this bill at the third reading.
Why I think they can have some confidence in what has been put in place are the
safeguards that were put in place at the Tr ansport and Industrial Relations Committee. I
understand the Greens were very constructive at  the select committee in helping to put
those safeguards in place. Having done that, and having done the best job possible, then
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5779
I would have thought that they are now in a position where, putting aside their
overwhelming principles, they could then support this bill, because this does not happen
very often. If you look at what this is about, then I think that maybe this was an
occasion when they could have put aside their objections.
I think the safeguard of a review panel that is  able to scrutinise the Orders in Council
and report to Parliament every 6 months is a very good one. Also, Parliament can
disallow the Orders in Council within 12 sitt ing days. That means the power still comes
back here to Parliament. Also, there is th e putting in place of a community committee
that is able to be involved in the design of  the park, to involve those local people who
will be affected. That is something that they were keen to see happen, and I am glad that
it has now become part of this project.
This is a really good idea. I want to pay tr ibute to the former Prime Minister of New
Zealand the Rt Hon Helen Clark. She had a passion—a burning passion—to ensure that
we remembered those men and women who ha d fought in many conflicts on behalf of
New Zealanders. Over her years as Prime Mini ster, there were a number of things that
she did to ensure that our ol d soldiers were recognised. One of them, of course, was the
return of the Unknow n Warrior and the Tomb of th e Unknown Warrior. It was a
wonderful occasion for New Zealand, and for this Parliament, when the body of the
Unknown Warrior was brought back to New Zealand and lay in state here in Parliament,
and then was taken on Armistice Day down to where the park will be. It was estimated
that over 100,000 people lined the streets to see the body go past. It was a very moving
ceremony, and it showed the depth of feeling that New Zealanders have towards those
who have paid the price to ensure that we  have democracy, free speech, and freedom in
this country.
I want to not only say thank you to the fo rmer Prime Minister but also acknowledge
that, belatedly, this Government has picked up the idea. I think it is a shame that we
waited so long. Money was allocated for this park; I was Minister of Transport at the
time. Along with Helen Clark, the Minist er for Arts, Culture and Heritage, we
announced $10.9 million in 2007 for this park. It was then stopped after the election,
and nothing happened for a long ti me. In fact, it was a piece of land that lay there bare,
with an old fence around it, and lots of pa per bags and plastic bags blowing across it.
Finally, a decision was made to proceed. Well done. I am glad that it is proceeding. It
will be opened in April 2015, and I hope that at that time we can all come together and
commemorate what is going to be a very signi ficant project for all New Zealanders. We
strongly support this bill and look forward to its completion with as much speed as
possible.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia ora. I rise to
take a call on the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill, which is
now in its third reading. I f eel like we have been speaking about it a bit la tely in this
House, because we have. With the speed at  which this bill has gone through its first
reading, through a very fast select committee process, through the second reading,
through the Committee stage, and now the third reading, we have been talking about it a
lot so I feel well versed in some of the issues. But I still have not heard anyone from the
Government benches talk abou t the real reasons why we have to go through this
extraordinary step of passing legislation to get a park—the extraordinary step of passing
legislation to get a park. We  have created parks for more  than 100 years pretty well
without legislation in the past, and the Greens would prefer to keep it that way.
I would like to elaborate and say, as we ha ve said in the numerous stages of the
debate, that the Green Party supports the es tablishment of this park. We would support
it through its normal processes; we want to  see it completed in time for the 100 th
anniversary of the Gallipoli landings fo r Anzac Day commemorations in 2015. We
5780 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
think that as well as providing New Zeal anders and our Aussie Anzac cousins who
come, and our overseas visitors, a tranquil place to enjoy throughout the year, it would
be an amazing way to commemorate the 100 th anniversary of those landings, which
some people say is when New Zealand came of age, which obviously  was a significant
milestone. It is also an oppor tunity to remember all thos e servicemen who have died,
who are commemorated around this Chamber.
But the Green Party will not be supporting this  bill in its third reading because of the
process issues, because we are going throu gh this extraordinary step of passing
legislation to get a park. We do not think it is worthwhile, and we still have not heard
from the Government benches—and less so fr om the Labour benches, as well. I do not
blame them; I think they did it appropriately by announcing it in 2004, because they put
money behind it. But no one on the Government side has said why they—remember,
they were the Government at that time— scrapped the funding in 2009. If they were
such huge supporters of the park, why did they  scrap the funding? It is the question that
those on the Government benches do not want to talk about, and of course they do not
want to talk about it because it is embarrassing.
I agree that New Zealanders and Wellington ians of all persuasions want to see a
park. We want to see a respectful war memo rial. We want to see it in time for 2015, but
we do not want to see an abuse of process. I still have not heard from the Government
benches why we have to pass legislation to  see it by 2015. If there is such astounding
goodwill amongst the community—and I acknowle dge the support of the council,
including the commitment of  $5 million, and the support, including from the Green
Party, to see the outcomes—why do we have to pass legislation? We still have a number
of years before the anniversary. Let us not  forget that we have known about this
anniversary for 97 years. What we know is that the Government—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Oh, there’s always a few crazies  to hold the process up. That’s
why the Green Party’s in existence!

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Simon Bridges is quite happy to talk in interjections about the
Green Party, but he refuses to talk about  why his Government scrapped the funding in
2009, why his party has to abuse the process,  and why his party has to go through the
extraordinary step of passing such laws. I am sure that the member, who is also a
learned lawyer, would prefer to see, in respec t of some of the more important pieces of
legislation crowding out the Order Paper, so me actual achievement there. What we are
doing is passing a bill to get a park, and there is a huge oppo rtunity cost. What this bill
does, obviously, is override the Resource Management Act, the Historic Places Act, and
the Public Works Act. It gives the Crow n the powers, through Order in Council,
essentially to do whatever it wants to get this park achieved. We are concerned about
the precedent this sets for further legislati on. We are concerned about the trend from
this Government, which can be seen in this legislation.
Of course, the Government talks about consultation because it has to—it is a
statutory obligation on many functions—bu t this Government does not genuinely
believe in consultation, I believe. You can see it in the earthquake legislation, which has
extraordinary powers of the highest degree  and where the Minister for Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery has extr aordinary powers. We can s ee it in the way Government
members have approached controversial tran sport projects. They do not want to hear
from the community. They do not want to ha ve a real conversation about what are the
alternatives—how do we have smarter transport options. All they want to do is ram
things through a fast-tracked  Environmental Protection Agency process where people’s
rights to have a say are seve rely constrained. The rights of appeal are virtually non-
existent because people can appeal only on points of law.
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5781
But let us get to th e good stuff. I would like to acknowledge the members of the
Transport and Industrial Rela tions Committee. I would like  to thank the submitters.
Both groups, we have to note,  went through a very fast-tra cked process. I think there
was only a week between the first reading and the closing of submissions. We would
like to acknowledge them and thank them, but note that it was a very fast process. We
are very concerned that the trend seen in th is bill is being abused by this Government
and that is why we are not going to support it.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: We haven’t done any late-night urgency in this Parliament.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Well, we are not seeing late-n ight urgency because we have
got the—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: I miss it.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: The member Simon Bridges interjects about late-night
urgency. It is because we have the support of the House to go through a new process
called extended hours to deal with legisla tion of a non-controversial nature. Obviously
this is pretty controversial, because we are not doing it in extended hours. What we
know, though, is that we still have a signifi cant number of bills on the Order Paper—
important parliamentary work that we shoul d be getting down to, but instead we are
passing laws to get a park. It is absolutely extraordinary. We have known about it for 97
years. The Government refuses to talk about the real reasons why we have to go through
this extraordinary step. It is because it stopped the funding.
I would like to quickly comment on the comments by the member Annette King that
it would be nice to have unanimous support. We agree, it would be nice to have
unanimous support. However, there was a bett er way to go about th is: a better way that
did not mean we have to set aside a number of laws; a better way that did not mean we
have to give the Minister ex traordinary powers to do whatev er he or she wants through
Order in Council. But I have got to take exception to the comment made by the member
Annette King that the Greens should put asid e their principles and support the bill. The
one thing the Green Party will not be doing is putting aside our principles. We will
never put aside our principles. To the Green Party, that is the core of why we are in this
House. This is why New Zealanders voted for us in record numbers at the last election,
because they want some principle in this House. They do not want the tired pragmatism,
the petty point-scoring, the tribal battle across the House.
They want some principle, and the Greens will not be putting aside our principle.
[Interruption] The House is riled up now, that is good. I will let the members quieten
down for a second, because I would like to finish on a serious note. I would like to
finish on a serious note.
I would like to finish with a comment made  in today’s newspaper about this. I would
like to finish with the comments of histor ian and journalist Dr Rachel Buchanan from
today’s paper, which I think sums up exactly why the Greens are taking this principled
approach. Dr Buchanan says: “Pukeahu is a subtle, powerful, significant site and this
place deserves to be treated with more re spect than this draconian empowering bill
seems to allow.” We will continue to vote with  principle, we will continue to support
this park, but we will not be supporting this abuse of process. Kia ora, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: That speech by Gareth Hughes
was just totally inappropriate for this  National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu)
Empowering Bill, and it shows the level of incompetence in the Green Party. It is not a
party of principle; it is merely a moon th at goes round “Planet Labour”. It has achieved
nothing, will never achieve anything, and will do nothing in this Parliament, because it
can never, ever be part of a Government, and because its members are objectors and that
is all they are.
5782 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
This is a bill that has actually had real  consultation and real listening between the
parties involved in the Transport and Indus trial Relations Committee, and I would like
to thank all the parties that were on the se lect committee and that worked constructively
together. I thank especially the members of the select committee, our Minister of Arts,
Culture and Heritage, and also the Labour Party members for their work in this area.
This is a bill where we did have cons ultation and where we brought the community
in. We actually changed the bill to give the community more avenues for further
consultation and effectiveness in the implementa tion of this bill. It is good work of this
Parliament, it is for a good cause, and it was done to get this project completed by the
time of a very important day in our history. It  is time that this Parliament supported this
bill, and even the most principled approach should be one of support. Thank you.

items.speaker: ANDREW WILLIAMS
items.text: I take a call on behalf of New Zealand First as
the veterans affairs spokesperson for New Zealand First for the National War Memorial
Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. We have sp oken on this on a number of occasions in
the last few days and it is very pleasing to s ee this come for its third reading. I have had
the privilege over the years when travelling around the world to visit many very special
places of commemoration to do with our loved ones who have lost their lives on behalf
of New Zealand, on behalf of  the Commonwealth, fighting for our country. I can recall
a few years ago being in Flanders in Be lgium and going to the Tyne Cot Cemetery,
where so many New Zealanders are buried an d where the silver fern is on so many
white headstones. It is a special place wher e the quietness, the solitude, and the peace
are really something, and it is quite an am azing experience to be there. And when you
compare that to many other such memorial parks around the work in great capitals and
in great cities around the wo rld, you see that, similarly, their memorials and their
cenotaphs are given a high level of respect, a nd are in an appropriate  position, as they
are in cities such as Washington, DC, London, Sydney, Canberra, and many other great
cities of the world where their memorial parts are very much of significance. Just
recently we were in Melbourne and were  most impressed with the cenotaph in
Melbourne and the wonderful large tomb th ere that you go into  in Melbourne. The
peace and serenity of the whole place was magnificent.
So here in Wellington, our capit al city, it is somewhat unf ortunate that our National
War Memorial, our national Cenotaph, the National War Memorial Carillon, and the
Tomb of the Unknown Warrior have a major State highway, State Highway 1, marching
right across the face of them, with busy traffi c noise, which is not conducive to what
should be a very respected place for our nati on. So this National War Memorial Park is
to be completed by 2015 for the 100 th commemoration of the Gallipoli situation of
World War I, and it is most fitting that this  is completed and that we have a National
War Memorial Park with an area of green, an area of planted gardens,  of trees, and of
just peacefulness, so that those national memorials and the national Cenotaph do have a
much better backdrop than the current roading situation.
It is very pleasing that the Australian G overnment is recognising the significance as
well, alongside us, as our Anzac friend, and pr oviding $5 million towards it to include
an Australian memorial within the park to mark that sign ificance between Australia and
New Zealand and of how many Au stralian and New Zealand sold iers lost their lives at
Gallipoli and in many other theatres of war.
It is unfortunate that the Green Party is not  supporting this because of the process. It
is understandable that the process has been  pressure-cooked and steamrolled somewhat
to get this done, but we cannot miss the d eadline, we cannot miss 2015 for the Gallipoli
commemorations, and we cannot risk there be ing any hold-ups on it. So in situations
like this there are certain circumstances wh ere really there shoul d be full cross-party
support to ensure that we get this completed.
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5783
Moving a major road—trenching it and undergrounding it—is no simple task, and
there will be a major component in it that ha s to be done. They do not want to have any
hiccups with it, because it would be a great shame if they did not meet the deadline and,
therefore, the whole essen ce of getting it done by the 100 th anniversary would be lost.
So in that respect New Zealand First does s upport this. We will gi ve it all our support
and we will ensure that we lend whatever s upport we can to the Government and to all
the other parties—to the Wellington City Council, to the RSA and Veterans Affairs—to
ensure that this can be expedited in the fastest manner possible so that we will all be
very proud as New Zealanders in 2015 to have a very fitting park of national standard.
But at the same time, as I mentioned in  the House yesterday, we cannot just be
reliant on marking the 100 th year of Gallipoli, of marking the recognition of those who
have fallen on behalf of this country, and of marking a significant part of our history of
New Zealand without also recognising that we  still have issues around veterans’ affairs
here today, and tomorrow. There are still veterans in this country who are suffering as a
result of going off to many of those theatr es of war—going off to  Korea, going off to
Malaya, going off to Viet Nam, and going off to other more recent theatres of war. They
have issues around their health, around their family health, and around various things
that occurred to them during their time of service. So a lthough this project is putting
$12 million towards the park, and then, of c ourse, a more significant, $70 million - odd
to underground State Highway 1, that is a si zable chunk of money, a nd I would like to
think that at the same time, while we ar e giving strong, multiparty, support to getting
this project done, there would be increased mu ltiparty support, and certainly significant
support from Government circles, to recognise the affair s of veterans who are alive and
with us today and who need a lot more support than they are currently being afforded.
In that respect, as I mentioned also yest erday, the War Pensions Act review that was
carried out 2 years ago by the Law Co mmission made 170 recommendations for a
review of various conditions for our veterans. New Zealan d First would like to see
much more progress, much faster progre ss, on that review being enacted. We are
continuing to ask the Government to m ove on that. Many of these veterans are
becoming very elderly, very sick, and their wives and families are suffering as well.
Their wives and families and t hose around them are being aff ected as a result. We do
have a duty of care in this Parliament and in this country to ensure that our veterans are
also being well taken care of. So let us sort out the bricks and mortar of the park, sort
out the bricks and mortar of the Cenotaph, the National War Memorial, and the Tomb of
the Unknown Warrior, but let us  not forget the living flesh that is here today, the
veterans who also similarly need that fi nancial support and need that moral support
from this Parliament to also take care of them. In closing, New Zealand First supports
this bill and we welcome this third reading being completed today.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—T āmaki): I think the place of memory is
incredibly important. I was struck over th e weekend, as I was joining the Scouts of
Glendowie and St Heliers celebrating their 10 0-year anniversary, that they drew my
attention towards a little water fountain that sits in St Helie rs as a memorial to one of
their first Scoutmasters, Guyon Brookfield, who served and died. Awareness of that
memorial was being reignited, if you like, in th e young people of today, and they are
being made aware of it, and th ey were able to connect with  that. It reminded me that
that is just a small-scale version of what we are talking about here today: a National
War Memorial to all our war dead, throughout a variety of wars, and the importance of
allowing their memory to live on in our hearts  and minds. I think it is very important
that we come together as one House to support this bill, the National War Memorial
Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill, and I encour age our colleagues in the Green Party to
support this bill. Principles are important, but principles do not exist in a vacuum. So
5784 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
once again I encourage the House to join in  one voice to remember those who have
served this country so finely.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: The arguments for and
against and around this piece of legislation, the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu)
Empowering Bill, have been well rehearsed in the House over the last few days and
weeks. We know the situation. The situation is that despite the fact that the building of
the war memorial park is a commemoration of the centenary of the landings at Gallipoli,
we find ourselves in a position where we do need to rush through legislation and
legislate for a rushed process by which the park can be built. We know that that has
come about because a vision and a plan that  was started in 2004 and was in place by
2008 was brought to a halt by the current Govern ment. We know that what is necessary
is to assist the Government to get out of that  difficult position it has put itself in, and to
make progress towards ensuring that our vete rans are appropriately honoured by having
the park constructed and indeed the full National War Memorial completed in time for
those centennial commemorations on 25 April 2015.
We also know that the Greens have put themselves in an interesting position of
saying that they support the park and they  support the concept, but are opposing the
legislation. They would say that is a principl ed position. What sorts of principles would
support not getting this park in place in time? They have no t answered the question that
I asked yesterday, I think it was, or the day before, about what they would do if it was
up to them, if their vote was going to carry this legislation. I think that is perhaps a
broader philosophical question that the Greens need to answer for themselves.
But as hard as I ha ve been on the Greens about their position on this  legislation, I
also just want to take up David Bennett’s rath er glossy synopsis of what this legislation
is about. He said that this is an example of ideal consultation. It is not. Let us not try to
make this legislation into something that it is not.

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: We don’t want to put lipstick on the pig.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Not on David Bennett’s pig, no. But what we need to
acknowledge is that this  is getting the Government out of  a situation that it created for
itself that it did not need to create. As much  as Labour supports the legislation in order
to ensure that the war memorial is completed on time, let us not glos s over the fact that
the Government got itself into this position when it absolutely did not need to.
I want to take up a different issue related to this war memorial that has been brought
to my attention over the last 2 days. That is  the fact that there is a small minority of
people out there who believe that a war memorial itself is an abomination, that it
somehow glorifies war, and that we are somehow celebrating conflict and death through
the construction of a war memorial. Nothing co uld be further from the truth. I challenge
those people who have offered that opinion to  me to attend any of the commemorations
of the different conflicts that New Zealan ders have been invol ved in over the last
century. There are a number of them now. Along with other members of the House I
have attended several this year. I want t hose people who hold that opinion to know that
they are sombre occasions where the sacrif ice and the service of  the people who went
and served our nation, many of whom did not come home, and many of whom did come
home but were utterly changed by the experi ence, are acknowledged. It is in no way a
glorification of conflict. I think of the e xperience of watching elderly men and women
weeping in memory of their fallen comrades.
Just this week I heard the Minister of Veterans’ Affair s, Nathan Guy, mention that
many of us shared some time with the veterans of Bomber  Command at the war
memorial this week. One of the speakers th ere recounted the expe rience of waking up
some mornings to find that their room-mate’ s bed had not been slept in, and that meant
only one thing. That meant that their room-mat e had not come home that night and that
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5785
they were lost. That is an experience that  was some 70 years ago now, and yet that
gentleman was moved to tears. I have heard a number of veterans recount tales that are
similar to that. That in no way tries to sugge st that we glorify c onflict. That shows the
true humanity of conflict and reminds us as a nation why it is important to avoid
conflict at all costs, and to seek a diplomatic and peaceful solution to the conflicts that
nations might have. These days it is often not nations warring against each other; it is
often non-State participants in conflict that we  have to work with and deal with, and try
to find solutions to the things that divide us.
So I think having a war memorial is an important component of that memory,
because if we forget those conf licts, if we forget what it is like to send people to war
and not have them come home again, then we are in danger of putting ourselves in that
situation once again without being fully cognisant of what it is that we are doing. That is
something, I know, that all New Zealanders ar e acutely aware of at  the moment, given
the fact that we have suffered the pain of lo sing our armed forces personnel, especially
over the last 2 years in Afghanistan. So I think it is important that we complete the
National War Memorial, that we do it in an appropriate way, that we do it in a way that
honours our fallen and those who returned, and that we create a space that recognises all
the sacrifices of war, including, I have to say, the sacrifices made by those who were
conscientious objectors. Absolutely, they we re people who had the right to object to
war. Certainly, we can debate the merits of the different c onflicts that we have sent
people to over the years. But ultimately the people who go and serve, their job is not to
debate the rights and wrongs of conflict; their job is to go and serve the will of their
nation and serve the will of the Government of the day. I think an important aspect of
this park is that there will be a space to acknowledge the conscientious objectors, and
that it will be a quiet and peaceful place to reflect on the nature of sacrifice. Certainly, at
the moment, the war memorial is not a quiet and peaceful place, when you are outside it
with all the traffic flowing past.
There is one more thing that I think is important to acknowledge at this point, and
Andrew Williams touched on this as well. There is one further way in which we need to
acknowledge the service and sacr ifice of our veterans, and th at is to modernise the War
Pensions Act 1954. It was on Tuesday, 1 June  2010, more than 2 years ago, that the
Law Commission presented its re port to Parliament. It is a very fulsome report—it has
170 recommendations in it—and it is unders tandable that the Government has taken
some time to deal with that report, but 2 years is too long. The right way to honour our
veterans is to ensure that we have mode rn, contemporary, and a ppropriate legislation
that ensures our veterans are being taken car e of appropriately, because their service is
greater, and the likelihood that they are injured, or ill, as a result of their service is much
greater, than it is for the gene ral population. It is unfortunate and very, very sad that we
have not been able to do more, and that th is Government has not been able to do more,
to honour our veterans.
So in closing we celebrate the fact that the war memorial will be completed in time
to commemorate the centenary of the Gallip oli landings, and we l ook forward to much
faster action from the Government in terms of doing something real and tangible for our
veterans by revamping the War Pensions Act.

items.speaker: SCOTT SIMPSON
items.text: In just over 2 years and some
months, 25 April 2015 will be the day that our nation commemorates the 100 th
anniversary of the Gallipoli landing at Anzac C ove. Both my grandfathers served there.
Both, fortunately, came home, although one was wounded, and—can you believe it—
was patched up and then sent to Passche ndaele before coming home. At Gallipoli
103,000 New Zealanders served, 50,000 were  wounded, and 18,500 made the ultimate
5786 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 27 Sep 2012
sacrifice. At the time we had a country w ith a population of just over 1 million people.
That was a sacrifice almost intolerable to bear.
So nearly 100 years on it is with great pride and, I guess,  expectation that I support
the passage of this legislation, the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering
Bill, through the House. I want to commend the work of the Transport and Industrial
Relations Committee and the diligent chairm anship of David Bennett, who has guided
this legislation through the select committ ee process. I am looking forward, along with
all other New Zealanders, to seeing this new memorial park built in time for the
commemorations on 25 April 2015, and I commend this bill to the House with pride and
expectation. Thank you.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Well, I do not think I need the 10 minutes. Thank
you for that opportunity. I raced down to the H ouse because I was really keen to take a
call on the third reading of the National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering
Bill. I have seen this, along with other members of the Transport and Industrial
Relations Committee, through the process, and very hasty it was t oo. But it was a very
constructive process, I have to say. It is on e of those rare moments in the House when
you feel good about something that we actuall y are voting on. It has not happened very
often recently. So I am really pleased that La bour is supporting this bill, and that we are
going to have as a result of it a wonderfu l National War Memorial Park, which will be
built in time for the 100th anniversary of Gallipoli in 2015.
I have heard other members talking about their experiences of visiting Gallipoli.
Well, I have not done that; I hope one day that  I get over that wa y. But what I have
done, and I mentioned it in my second readin g speech, is I have visited Flanders and I
have visited the sites of ma ny of the famous battles in World War I—of Passchendaele,
Ypres, and Messines. When we were in Messi nes, quite recently, we were told that the
remains of a First World War soldier ha d been found—someone from the Battle of
Messines. It had just happened accidentall y. Contractors had been digging a ditch and
they came across the remains of a soldier. That was incredible—95 years after that
battle they are still findi ng the remains of people who fought. It has now been
confirmed, since I was there, that it was a New Zealand First World War soldier who
fought in the battle who has been disc overed. The remains were found alongside two
New Zealand infantry soldier badges in Messines, as I have said, where New Zealand
troops were involved in intense fighting in World War I.
It is really poignant to think that 95 y ears later we are still finding the remains of
soldiers who fought in those dr eadful battles of World War I.  I could not he lp thinking,
now I see that it has been confirmed th at he was around 25 year s old, how unbelievable
it must have been for the mother, being th e mother of a son myself, to say goodbye to
her young son and to never hear from him ag ain—never to hear from him again. Of
course, that family is no longer there a nd they cannot confirm the identity. The only
good news about that is that he will be reburied. He will be buried alongside his
comrades from the First World War, in an  appropriate Commonwealth war grave. So I
think that when we get to the celebra tion and commemoration in 2015, I will be
thinking about that 25-year-o ld. You know, I feel close to him, because I was there
when they found his remains and his body. As I said the other day, hundreds and
hundreds of people lost their lives—New Zealand boys, young boys—in that battle.
This New Zealand soldier will be buried with  a concrete plaque that will say “Known
only to God”. That is just unbelievably sa d, is it not? And there are many like that—
from the First World War, in particular.
27 Sep 2012 National War Memorial Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill 5787
So commemorating Gallipoli, Messines, Ypres, Verdun, and all of the battles that our
troops were involved in in th e First World War, is incred ibly important, because there
are family histories and there are family connections, whether or not you agree with
war—and I certainly do not. I think it is a reminder for us all to pay respects to the
memory of people who went to war believing that they were going to make a difference,
and that it was about democracy  and fighting injustice. I certainly will look forward to
the memorial park celebration in April 2015. Th is is a wonderful park, which we have
agreed among ourselves in this Parliament , apart from the concerns of the Greens,
should be built. It is a place where we can contemplate the lives of people like the 25-
year-old in Messines—the lives lost—but also think about peace and talk about peace. I
came away from Messines and those places fee ling more strongly than ever that that
was an awful war and it should never happen again.
If nothing else, this National War Memorial Park will be about our determination as
a nation to fight and make sure that there is  never again a war of that magnitude. It was
a futile war where our sons were sent away, lost to their mothers, not named, and buried
in foreign graves. In many ways this memorial  park will pay tribut e to those who have
given their lives, but who have also become a part of our history, a part of our blood,
and a part of who we are as a nation. So I am really pleased to be able to support this
bill in the third reading. I think, as I said, it is good. It is one of the good days in
Parliament when you can celebrate or agr ee on something that is worthwhile and
something that we all believe in. This is something that we all believe we need to do for
the memory of those who have gone before. Thanks.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is a privilege to take this last call on this
very important bill, the National War Memori al Park (Pukeahu) Empowering Bill. As a
former serviceman, whose father, Lew Sa bin, and my uncle, Lew Gibb, were also
former servicemen, this bill holds a special  place with me. Can I just acknowledge all
current and all former servicemen, in particular, and those who have given their lives so
that we have the freedoms that we enjoy to day. Can I make clear the reverence that I
hold, certainly this party holds, and, indeed, all New Zealanders hold for those men and
women who have made the ultimate sacrifice.
Anzac Day truly does epitomise the very special place in the hearts of New
Zealanders that these veterans and servic emen, and current servicemen, occupy. This
bill really is about providing the mechanic s to ensure that in 2015, on Anzac Day, we
have an appropriate place to pay homage to those people who have laid their lives down
for us, and those who have served in wars and come home, and carry those scars with
them for ever.
This bill is about ensuring that we have a place to celebrate for them. The politics
that have been played out today are not what is important here. Those people are special
to us. This place will be spec ial to us. They have made sa crifices, lest anyone in this
House or this nation forget. I commend this bill to the House.
