items.speaker: Minister of Commerce
items.text: I move, That the Commerce (Inter national Co-operation, and
Fees) Amendment Bill, the Credit Contract s and Consumer Finan ce (International Co-
operation) Amendment Bill, the Fair Tradi ng (International Co-operation) Amendment
Bill, and the Telecommunications (International  Co-operation) Amendment Bill be now
read a third time . The legislation plays an important role in supporting the
Government’s objective of a single economic market with Australia. It builds on other
single economic market initiatives progres sed by the Government over the past 12
months, such as the Trans-Tasman Proceedings Act. The aim of this legislation is to
facilitate enhanced cooperation between the Commerce Commission and the Australian
Competition and Consumer Commission and ot her overseas competition and consumer
regulators. The legislation aims to achie ve this by enabling the Commerce Commission
to use its statutory powers and information acquired through use of its statutory powers
to assist the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and overseas regulators
in other countries. This in turn should enhance the commission’s ability to obtain
assistance from overseas regulators for its own investigations.
I would like to quickly outline some of the key features of the regime in the
legislation. Firstly, the proposed amendments  operate on the princi ple of reciprocity.
This should ensure that cooperation arrangements under the legislation result in benefits
to New Zealand. Secondly, the legislation provi des flexibility in the type of cooperation
arrangements to be used. By allowing both Government to Government and regulator to
regulator types of agreements , it allows us to tailor our  approach to cooperation
agreements with different c ountries as is appropriate. Thirdly, and very important,
although the regime enhances the commission’ s ability to assist overseas competition
and consumer regulators, it re cognises that in doing so ther e need to be appropriate
public interest safeguards.
The legislation provides such safeguards at  two levels. Firstly, it does so through
requiring specific matters to be taken into account at a ministerial level. Such matters
are broad, and include having regard to the legal framework in the overseas country and
the potential consequences to New Zealand businesses and consumers of a cooperation
arrangement. Secondly, and separately, once a cooperation arrangement is in place, the
legislation requires specific matters to be considered by the co mmission on a case by
case basis. Providing safeguards at both levels is important in ensuring that appropriate
consideration is given to pub lic interest matters at diffe rent stages. It should also
promote confidence in the integrity and implementation of cooperation arrangements
under the legislation.
Overall, the legislation further implements the Government’s commitment to making
further progress towards a si ngle economic market with Au stralia. In doing so, the
legislation equips the commission with modern-day tools to combat anti-competitive
behaviour and enforce consumer laws in the international context of business today.
I would like to thank everyone who has cont ributed to the legi slation, including the
members of the Commerce Committee, the Parl iamentary Counsel Office, officials, and
the members of the public and industry representatives who participated in the various
submission and policy processes. I want also  to acknowledge other parties in the House
for their support of this legislation.
I commend these bills to the House, and move that they be read a third time.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: After that third reading
contribution on the Commerce (International Co-operation, and Fees) Amendment Bill,
the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finan ce (International Co-operation) Amendment
27 Sep 2012 Third Readings 5789
Bill, the Fair Trading (International Co-operation) Amendment Bill, and the
Telecommunications (International Co-operation) Amendment Bill from the member
Simon Bridges, the whole House has realised just how important this legislation is to
the Government’s agenda. We have heard from the member, and he has spoken about
how important this is in terms of the mutual relationships with Australia, and how
important it is for business. It is so important that it was introduced on 9 September
2008 by me, when I was the Minister of Commer ce. That is how long it has been on the
Order Paper.
Admittedly, that was just prior to a ge neral election, so we were not expecting,
really, to see it dealt with within the firs t 100 days. Of course, the Government had its
own agenda for the first 100 days. Everyone  knows that giving anyone 100 days to do
something is a political statement, and that ev ery party is judged as it takes office on its
first 100 days. So we were not expecting this legislation to get its first reading within
the Government’s first 100 days. We understa nd that. We expect that. So when did it
get its first reading? Did it get its first reading just after the 100 days was up? No? Well,
maybe the second 100 days? Did it get it w ithin the second 100 days? Or maybe the
third 100 days, or the fourth 100 days, or th e fifth 100 days? That would be getting up
there. But, no, this legislation got its first reading on 25 May 2010—2010. So it was
actually quite a long way after the Government was elected to office. Yet we have heard
how important this legislation is.
Maybe it got held up at the Commerce Comm ittee. You know, it had its first reading
back in May 2010, and, I mean, we are dealing with it in 2012. So maybe it was held up
by that select committee, which was by that st age chaired by me. I was the chair of the
Commerce Committee when this legislation was referred to it. I was the Minister who
introduced the Commerce Commission (International Co-operation, and Fees) Bill, and
I subsequently become the chair of the select committee that received the bill on 25
May 2010. Maybe I was a bit slack, and maybe we  did not deal with the bill as quickly
as we should have. When did submissions on th at bill close? Submissions on that bill
closed on 30 June 2010. So we gave a reasonable time for people to make submissions
on it, and we reported back the bill—this is probably what has been the hold-up—on 22
November 2010. So actually we held that bi ll for less than the 6 months—well, no,
about the 6 months—that we would normally exp ect to have a bill for, and we reported
it back within that 6-month period. So, actually, we did our job.
So when did it get its second reading? We ll, it must have been in 2011. Surely it got
its second reading in 2011. Maybe there have been other things that have been holding
it up. But, actually, no, I went back and checked that. The second reading was on 3 May
2012—2012. The Committee stage was closely after that, on 29 May, and then
concluded on 31 July. And here we are now  on 27 September 2012. For legislation that
is so important to the Government—as we ha ve heard from the Mi nister, speaking on
behalf of the Minister who inhe rited it from the last Minister, who inherited it from the
Minister before, who was me—it actually has had quite a circular route to this point.
But I do want to say that we do support this legislation, and I do want to say that we
improved the quality of the legislation w ithin the context of the select committee
hearings as well.
It is not often that Parliament addresses legislation that has a degree of retrospectivity
included within it that is not subject to a New Zealand Bill of Rights Act vet, as is the
case in this particular instance. But, actually, the select committee amended the
definition of “compulsorily acquired” to ma ke it absolutely crystal clear that it was
retrospective in this regard. We were worried that the definition as introduced could
lead to existing information being excluded by the presumption agai nst retrospectivity,
and we did not want that to happen. We wanted to make it  clear that a ll compulsorily
5790 Third Readings 27 Sep 2012
acquired information would be subject to this, because the guidance was there in the
agreements that it had to be  subject to ministerial appr oval, either Government to
Government or regulator to regulator.
We had a long discussion about Governme nt to Government and regulator to
regulator approval as well, because, of cour se, we have issues, for example, with
utilising our relationship with Australia, wher e different states have  different regulators
and, in some instances, an overarching one. So I think that it is im portant to have the
ministerial approval and to have the flexibility while maintaining appropriate
safeguards, and that is what we did as a select committee.
We did note that there was some concern, and the Minister actually referred to this in
his comments. He said that there was a c oncern expressed that New Zealand would be
sharing information with a c ountry or a regulato r without “reciprocity”—I was actually
looking forward to using that word myself in this debate, and he got there first—or the
fact that the information may not be treated as secure, or may not be secure once it
leaves New Zealand. Again, I th ink that it was pretty clea r in the advice that we
received from officials, and the advice th at we actually accepted, that New Zealand
simply would not enter into an arrangement that did not provide th e level of protection
that is required when one is dealing with this type of information.
The last issue that I just wanted to touc h on briefly—and I do not think that the whip
would terribly mind if I just touched on this matter briefly; I am just checking—was the
question of international trade interests being protected. There will be issues that arise
from time to time that will be subject to consideration by such a request for
compulsorily acquired information, where, in fact, it may not be in New Zealand’s trade
interests to have that information made  available. In those cases the Commerce
Commission would consult the Mi nister of Trade, after cons ultation with the Ministry
of Foreign Affairs and Trade, and then rely on a statement by the Minister of Trade as to
whether providing the information or assi stance would significantly prejudice New
Zealand’s international trade interests.  Then, basically, before providing such
information the commission would have to be  satisfied that the information would not
significantly prejudice New Zealand’s internati onal trade interests. I think that that
protection is a pretty strong protection, and one that certainly was well received, I think,
when we reported the Comm erce Commission (Internationa l Co-operation and Fees)
Bill to the House.
I will mention one other point, because I di d not get the nod from the whip that I was
looking for, and he is still not nodding. I just wanted to touch briefly on the question of
whether the statutory powers of compulsion that the commi ssion has can be used only
in relation to enforcement and adjudication within New Zealand, and there also being
legal constraints on the provi sion to overseas regulators of  confidential compulsorily
acquired information that is already held by the commission. I think that this does limit
the willingness of overseas regulators to provide assistance to the commission, as cross-
jurisdictional assistance tends to be based on that concept of mutual assistance or
reciprocity, as I have already mentioned.
I think that possibly I have got the nod now, so I think that  on that basis I would like
to say that I really did enjoy chairing the Commerce Committee when legislation like
this was supported across the House. I am certainly welcoming, after—well, since it
started its journey on 9 September 2008, it has ac tually just had its fourth anniversary.
So it is very pleasing to see it  finally receive its third reading and the support of all the
House.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity
to stand and speak in support of the bills we are looking at that were formerly parts of
the Commerce Commission (International Co -operation, and Fees) Bill, which is
27 Sep 2012 Third Readings 5791
touching on all of these five bills of inte rnational cooperation. I do thank the previous
speaker, the Hon Lianne Dalziel, for the hi story lesson—what a great grasp of figures
and dates. One of the things that we—

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Too much time on her hands.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I think so, too much time. In fact, if we had not detoured
through memory lane we might have got through this a lot faster, which is what she was
hoping.
It is important to understand  in this modern age of gl obal trade that things are
happening very, very rapidly, and especially as we see New Zealand and Australia lay
out their ultra-fast broadband. This creates  even greater opportuni ties for businesses on
both sides of the Tasman to cooperate and work together in a single economic market,
which, we know, is very important for us and is also very important for our Australian
brothers and sisters, or cousins, or whatever you may refer to them as, over the Tasman.
This legislation is going to allow that bett er trans-Tasman work. It is going to allow
enforcement of competition and consumer laws. This is incredibly important because
we know that an even playing field is what  competition thrives on, and when we have
good, honest competition we know that the consumer is the person who will benefit
most of all, because competition means efficiency in product development and
efficiency in marketing and sales because  everybody is competing for the consumer’s
interest. In the final analysis, when there is that competition, the consumer is getting the
best deal that is possible: hi gh-quality services at the best de al possible. This legislation
is going a long way to support that, and it is very good to see it progress here to its third
reading.
International cooperation between regulator s is becoming very much part of the
global market place. We know that as a nati on we are big, big traders internationally. I
think somewhere between 85 percent and 90 per cent of what we manufacture gets sent
overseas. We know that this legislation matters  a lot for us in terms of our ability to
interact on that global stage,  so it is important for its progress to go through the House
in this final reading. Our ambition is that  a New Zealand company can do business as
easily in Australia as it can at home, a nd vice versa. We know that as ultra-fast
broadband rolls out in Australia and in Ne w Zealand there will be that fantastic
opportunity for people to trade, interact, disc uss, make business plans, and cooperate as
if they were in the same room. We are yet to  see the advantage and the benefit of that in
our businesses, and I think it is going to be outstanding. I think it is going to see great
advancement for businesses in New Zealand.
So the easier we can make it for companies to operate in both countries, by removing
unnecessary barriers, the great er the opportunities will be for business to make big
productivity gains and take up the new oppor tunities that will underpin long-term
business growth. We know that New Zealand is in far better shape than many nations
around the world. We know that Australia ha s done very well during a time when many
other countries have struggled. So it is good that we can have this arrangement,
particularly with Australia, and other regulat ors as well, of course, so that we can
continue to build on the strengths that we have as a nation. I am very pleased to support
this. I think that this is going to be very  positive and progressive for businesses and also
for the regulators of both Australia and New Zealand. Thank you.

THURSDAY, 27 SEPTEMBER 2012 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
MOTIONS 
Ombudsmen, Office—50th Anniversary of Establishment 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Deputy Leader of the House) : Following discussion in the 
Business Committee, I seek leave to move G overnment motion No. 1. I move that this 
House place on record— 
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I had better put that leave to the House. Leave is sought for 
that purpose. Is there any objection? There is no objection. 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY : I move, That this House place on record that 1 October 
marks the 50 th anniversary of the establishment of the Office of Ombudsmen in New 
Zealand, the first in an English-speaking country and a model for the spread of the 
office throughout the world, and note the important contribution that the office makes to 
the preservation of administrative justice in this country. 
The Government is pleased to recognise the 50 th anniversary of the establishment of 
the Office of the Ombudsmen. The concept originated in Sweden in the early 19 th 
century. The Swedish Ombudsmen had juri sdiction over almost all national and 
municipal officials, who could be discip lined and even prosecuted for incorrect 
behaviour. Champions for establishing th e Ombudsman in New Zealand included 
National Party politicians John, or Jack, Marshall and Ralph Hanan. 
The Office of the Ombudsmen in New Zealand was established under the 
Parliamentary Commissioner (Ombudsman)  Act 1962 as an independent office 
protected by the authority of Parliament. This set an international precedent as in other 
countries Ombudsmen were appointed by th e Government. The first Ombudsman, Sir 
Guy Powles, a former lawyer, soldier, and diplomat, was sworn in  on 1 October 1962. 
He held the office until 1977. His performan ce made the institution widely respected, 
and its authority and scope were extended. The Ombudsmen Act 1975 allowed the 
appointment of several Ombudsmen, and thei r jurisdiction was ex tended to statutory 
boards and local government. Successive le gislation has solidified the Ombudsmen’s 
position. The 1982 Official Information Act,  the 1987 Local Government Official 
Information and Meetings Act, the Prot ected Disclosures Ac t 2000, and the Crown 
Entities Act 2004 have all added to the transparency of governing. 
New Zealand has been blessed to have had a succession of successful and influential 
Ombudsmen: Sir Guy Powles, Sir George Laking, Eaton Hurley, Lester Castle, Sir John 
Robertson, Nadja Tollemache, who was New Zealand’s first Ombudswoman, Susan 
Richards, Sir Brian Elwood, the Rt Hon Sir Anand Satyanand, Mel Smith, John 
Belgrave, and the two current Ombudsmen, Dame Beverley Wakem and David McGee. 
So on this 50 th anniversary we congra tulate them on all they do for New Zealand, and 
we look forward to the next 50 years. 
CHARLES CHAUVEL (Labour) : Since its creation half a century ago, the Office 
of the Ombudsmen has been occupied by a nu mber of truly gifted New Zealanders. The 
Deputy Leader of the House named them, a nd many of those names resonate with us 
still: Powles, our last Governor of Samoa; Laking, our ambassador to Washington in the 
years of the Kennedy and Johnson administrati ons; Robertson, a former State Services 
Commissioner, Secretary of De fence, and Secretary for Justice; Satyanand, a District 
Court judge who would go on to be Governor -General; Smith, a former Secretary for 
Justice; Belgrave, a former Secretary for Ju stice and also Secretary of Commerce, State 
5738 Motions 27 Sep 2012 
Services Commissioner, and Comptroller of  Customs; McGee, a long-serving and 
distinguished Clerk of this House; and, last, but of course not leas t, Wakem, previously 
Chief Executive of Radio New Zealand an d a member of the Higher Salaries 
Commission. These have all been  Officers of Parliament of  significant stature, who 
have served the public and our Parliament with distinction since 1962.  
The Ombudsmen perform an extremely impor tant role. As we look forward to the 
work of the office over the next 50 years we must all take seriously our responsibility as 
parliamentarians to ensure that it is properly resourced to do its job, and that we treat the 
office and its staff with the respect and the compliance that  the law properly demands. 
The Labour Opposition is pleased to support the motion. 
GARETH HUGHES (Green): Kia ora. Ng ā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia ora. I rise to 
support the motion on the 50 th anniversary of the establishment of the Office of the 
Ombudsmen. When New Zealand’s first Ombuds man, Sir Guy Powles, was sworn in in 
front of the Speaker of Parliament in 1962, he said “The Ombudsman is Parliament’s 
person—put there for the protection of the in dividual,”. New Zealand was the fourth 
country, after Sweden, Finland, and Denm ark, to establish the Office of the 
Ombudsmen, and was the first country outside of  Scandinavia. It is an idea that has 
caught on, and now, according to the International Ombudsman Institute, there are more 
than 150 countries with Ombudsmen-like institutions around the world.  
We would like to acknowledge the work of all the Ombudsmen, including the current 
two, Dame Beverley Wakem and Dr David Mc Gee, and also all the staff who have 
worked for them over the years. They play an important role in our democracy.  
However, we would also like to note the importance of adequate funding for them to 
be able to do that important role. In th e 2011 financial review of the Office of the 
Ombudsmen, the Chief Ombudsman stated that the office was in crisis and was now 
handling a significant increase in workloa d. We share what the member Charles 
Chauvel has said about the responsibility of all in Parliament to adequately fund the 
office.  
We have not agreed with every deci sion made by the Ombudsmen, and probably 
Governments have agreed even less, which I guess is testimony to the independence of 
the office. But I would like to share one positive example. In 2009 councils in Tasman 
and Canterbury were refusing to release im portant information regarding thousands of 
potentially contaminated toxic sites. As a result of the action by the Ombudsmen, that 
information is now public. We believe it was the right call, a nd it would not have 
happened without the intervention of the Ombudsmen. Fifty years on, we would like to 
acknowledge the establishment of this important office. Kia ora. 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) : New Zealand First joins with 
other parties in acknowledgi ng the celebration of this 50 th anniversary of the 
establishment of the Office of the Ombudsmen.  As has been said, to be correct, New 
Zealand was the first country outside of S candinavia to establish an Office of the 
Ombudsmen. Since then, the Office of the Om budsmen has come to play a significant 
role in our democracy.  
How ironic it is that we are marking this event this week. Thomas Jefferson said that 
the price of freedom is eternal vigilance. Th is week we have had a perfect illustration 
through the revelations of unlawful surv eillance activity of the Government 
Communications Security Bureau of the im portance of ensuring open, transparent, and 
accountable Government. We have been re minded that the great est threat to our 
democracy is secrecy and the abuse of power that occurs when the public are denied 
their right to know. Once again we have seen that those in  power are given to ignoring 
due process and the law, and that an effec tive democracy requires a range of supporting 
structures and institutions.  
27 Sep 2012 Motions 5739 
The Office of the Ombudsmen has proven a powerful mechanism for keeping the 
public informed, but there is a deeply tr oubling tendency for Government to apply 
obfuscation and delay in respond ing to Official Information Act requests, and all of us 
around here have been privy to  that. New Zealand First cons iders there is a strong case 
that additional funding should be allocated to  the Office of the Ombudsmen to ensure 
the public can gain access to official inform ation without the inordi nate delay that is 
often now the case. And probably the same sh ould be said about the Neazor report and 
that office, as well.  
It is appropriate that we mark the 50 th anniversary of the esta blishment of the Office 
of the Ombudsmen, because it plays a vital ro le in supporting democratic processes in 
New Zealand. 
Hon PETER DUNNE (Leader—United Future) : On behalf of United Future, I 
want to associate myself with the remarks that  have been made by others to first of all 
recognise and secondly congratulate the Offi ce of the Ombudsmen on the attainment of 
its 50th anniversary.  
When the office was established in 1962, times were much simpler, and the notion 
that there should be some sort of independent watchdo g able to ca ll Government 
agencies to account for actions where the in dividual citizen felt aggrieved was a pretty 
attractive one. For the first 20 years of th e office’s existence, that was largely its 
primary function. But the role of th e Office of the Ombudsmen has changed 
significantly since the advent of the Offici al Information Act, and the Ombudsman has 
become much more of an arbi ter of decisions as to whether or not certain information 
should be released. I often fear that that may be to the cost of the individual citizen. The 
aggrieved small person who wanted to take  an action before the Ombudsman may now 
find that the pressure from other claims, usua lly associated with Official Information 
Act requests in and around Government, is re ducing that authority. I am not saying that 
the two are inconsistent. I guess I am supporting the role of the office and the need for it 
to be resourced to do the job.  
Finally, can I conclude by no ting the high calibre of peopl e who have served in the 
role of Chief Ombudsman over the years. I have  had the privilege of working at various 
times with every one of them, bar Sir Guy Powles, and I think that they have all brought 
a uniformly high standard of integrity, intell igence, and perspicacity to the role. At the 
end of the day, what has made this office the success it has been, aped by so many other 
countries around the world but also now a revered New Zealand institution, has been the 
calibre of people who have served in that ro le. I think the challenge for this Parliament 
in the future when it appoints the next round of  Ombudspeople is to make sure that that 
consistently high standard is maintained and developed, and that the office in its next 50 
years continues to receive the respect that it deserves from the citizens of New Zealand. 
Motion agreed to. 
OBITUARIES 
Sir John Wallace, KNZM, QC 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader—NZ First) : I seek leave to move a motion 
without notice on the passing of Sir John Wallace, who, as you know, was the Chief 
Human Rights Commissioner, a High Court judge, and the chairman of the royal 
commission on the electoral reform structure that we now have.  
Mr SPEAKER : Leave is sought for that course of action. Is there any objection? 
There is no objection. 
Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS: I move, That this House note the passing of Sir John 
Wallace KNZM, QC, former Chief Human Ri ghts Commissioner, judge of the High 
5740 Obituaries 27 Sep 2012 
Court of New Zealand, and chairman of the Royal Commission on the Electoral System, 
which recommended the MMP system for se lecting elected members of Parliament . On 
behalf of New Zealand First, I wish to pay respects and to mark the passing of an 
eminent and distinguished New Zealander. Sir John made an outstanding contribution to 
public office in New Zealand in all the role s he fulfilled with distinction. As chairman 
of the Royal Commission on the Elec toral System, which recommended the 
introduction of MMP, Sir John made a lasting and profound difference to our 
parliamentary system and democracy. We extend our condolences to Sir John’s family. 
Motion agreed to. 
BUSINESS STATEMENT 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Deputy Leader of the House) : Next week the House is in a 
2-week adjournment. When the House resumes on Tuesday, 16 October, the 
Government will complete the Customs and Excise (Tobacco Products—Budget 
Measures) Amendment Bill and the Committee stages of the Taxation (Annual Rates, 
Returns Filing, and Remedial Matters) Bill, the Airports (Cost Recovery for Processing 
of International Travellers) Bill, and the Legislation Bill. Wednesday is a members’ 
day. 
Hon TREVOR MALLARD (Labour—Hutt South): Can the Deputy Leader of the 
House inform us as to whether it is sti ll the Government’s intention to make a little 
progress on the alcohol reforms the following week? 
Hon ANNE TOLLEY (Deputy Leader of the House): Depending on discussions in 
the Business Committee, the Alcohol Reform Bi ll is intended to retu rn to the House on 
23 October. 
POINTS OF ORDER 
Tabling of Documents—Accuracy of Description of Documents 
MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Senior Whip—National): I raise a point of order, Mr 
Speaker. It is in respect of  the tabling of documents. As  you know, we have discussed 
whether or not Speakers’ ruli ngs 147(4), (5), and (6) are being followed when there is 
the injection of commentary into the tabling of  documents. I raise this in respect of the 
documents tabled by the senior Opposition wh ip yesterday in response to an oral 
question to the Minister of Education, wh ere he paraphrased, and I quote—I will not 
quote exactly, but it is basically suggesting that  the Minister’s time frame would be 5 to 
6 weeks. On analysing the document when it was tabled, it eventuated that neither was 
it the Minister’s time frame nor was it in  respect of merger s and closures in 
Christchurch, but, in fact, of the special education review that was under way. I do not 
want to suggest to the House that the Oppositi on whip misled the House, or, if he did, 
that it was intentional, but I raise it as an example of the risks involved in the 
commentary that goes around the tabling of documents, and I would ask that you would 
again review that, with a view to curtailing the commentary that is attached to the leave 
that is sought. 
Mr SPEAKER : I think the point that is being ra ised is an interesting one. I ask 
members, naturally, to say sufficient about th e document to enable the House to make a 
rational decision about whether members shoul d allow it to be tabled. But I think the 
point is well made that that should not include  going into great detail of what is in the 
document. Members must be careful when they indicate what is in the document. I think 
members need to have some idea of what is in the document in order to make a decision 
about whether it should be tabled, but the need  for absolute accuracy  there is crucial. 
Seeking leave to table a document is an action of some formality. Members have 
27 Sep 2012 Points of Order 5741 
thought about the desire to seek leave. The House considers the matter, and gives leave. 
It is an important process. Therefore, careful thought should be given by members when 
they do indicate what is in a document. 
QUESTIONS FOR ORAL ANSWER 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Job Creation—Statistics and Reports 
1. DAVID BENNETT (National—Hamilton East)  to the Minister of Finance : 
How many jobs have been created in th e New Zealand economy over the past two 
years? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Associ ate Minister of Finance) on behalf of the Minister 
of Finance: Mr Speaker—[Interruption]  
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Order! I apologise to the Minister. The question contains no 
assertions of fact. It just asks a straight question. Before  the Minister had even opened 
his mouth, there was totally unacceptable interjection.  
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: A net 57,000 more New Zealande rs have a job now than 2 
years ago. That is according to the household labour force survey, seasonally adjusted, 
which is the standard internationally recognised measure of employment and 
unemployment.  
David Bennett : What examples has he seen of jobs being created in the 
infrastructure sector? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: Thanks to the Government’s  multibillion-dollar investment 
in infrastructure, afte r years of under-investment, and als o, of course, the Christchurch 
rebuild, many projects are bei ng undertaken to help crea te a faster-growing economy. 
Some specific examples include 1,000 new jobs over the next 4 years with the 
Waterview Connection construction, 1,000 new c onstruction jobs at Wiri Prison, nearly 
2,000 people in employment thanks to the ro ll-out of ultra-fast  broadband, and 1,000 
employed on the horizontal infrastructure re build in Christchurc h. Together, the total 
construction workforce required for the wide r Canterbury rebuild is estimated to be 
around 32,000.  
David Bennett : What examples has he seen of jobs being created in the 
manufacturing and information and communications technology sectors? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: The manufacturing sector has grown 6.1 percent by volume 
in the 2 years to June 2012. Some specific exam ples of jobs in this sector include the 
Continuous Catalyst Regeneration Project —which is just about to commence—at 
Marsden Point, which will employ around 350 people; the recommissioning of the 
second train at Methanex’s methanol plant in Taranaki, which has involved up to 500 
jobs; and the new, $200 million Fonterra plant at Darfield, which has involved more 
than 1,500 people during its construction. In the information and communications 
technology sector, examples include 400 new jobs in a pa rtnership between IBM and 
Unitec, 128 new jobs at Xero this calendar year, more than 100 new jobs at software 
company Orion Health, plus jobs at othe r great New Zealand exporting organisations 
like Tait Communications, Oktobor Animation, and many more.  
David Bennett: Has he seen any other examples of  projects that would create jobs 
that have not yet been able to proceed? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: The Minister has seen some examples of that. For example, 
a new international convention centre in Auckland would create around a thousand new 
jobs during its construction and around 800 jobs once it is up and running. Of course, 
that is being opposed as much as possibl e and slowed down by the Greens and Labour. 
Then there is the Bathurst Resources escarpment mine project on the West Coast, which 
5742 Questions for Oral Answer 27 Sep 2012 
would employ 225 people, if objectors withdrew  their appeals, of course. I would say 
again to the Amalgamated Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Union, Labour, and 
the Greens that if they were serious about  helping Coasters, th ey would call on 
opponents to drop their objections and allow this project to proceed. 
David Bennett : What reports has he seen about  support for jobs in the mining 
sector? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE : The Minister has seen three quite intriguing reports. The 
first, a recent statement, sa id “Let me be very clear here, I have always supported 
mining on the West Coast.”, the second said that “undeveloped coal reserves should be 
left in the ground.”, and the third said th at “Our position on mining has never been 
unclear and has always been consistent.” Those three statements came from Labour 
MPs Damien O’Connor, Maryan Street, and David Parker. 
Mr SPEAKER: The Hon Trevor Mallard. [ Interruption] Order! I want to hear this 
question. The Hon Trevor Mallard. 
Hon Trevor Mallard: Has he seen the letter from Or ion Health—which he referred 
to in a supplementary answer—to Craig Foss, the Minister of Commerce, indicating that 
its business had been placed at risk as a re sult of the decision of Mr Foss to override the 
unanimous decision of a select  committee of this House to  do with the patenting of 
software, and that its business could well go offshore as a result of that? 
Hon STEVEN JOYCE: No, I am not aware of a letter in that regard. I suggest that 
if the member has a question in that respec t he puts it down to Mr Foss, who is in 
charge of that portfolio. Also, from my br ief knowledge of the matter that the member 
raises, I do not think his assertion is correct, anyway. 
Hon David Parker: I seek leave to table a document compiled by the Parliamentary 
Library, which shows that th ere are more New Zealanders  unemployed as of June 2012 
than there were in June 2010. 
Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER : Leave is sought to table that document. Is there any 
objection? There is objection. 
Question time interrupted. 
PERSONAL EXPLANATIONS 
Tabling of Documents—Accuracy of Description of Documents 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Senior Whip—Labour) : I seek leave to correct a 
misrepresentation that has just been made— 
Mr SPEAKER : Order! Is the member seeking leave to make a personal 
explanation? 
CHRIS HIPKINS : Yes, that is right, to correct  a misrepresentation made by the 
senior Government whip. 
Mr SPEAKER: I think we have got to be a little  careful here. We have got to be a 
little careful with seeking leave to make a personal explanation. We had a situation 
yesterday where a member was granted leave and then started to talk about another 
political party. If the member is clear that he wishes to make a personal explanation 
because something has been said that is personally offensive to him, then I am perfectly 
happy to seek leave from the House for th at. If the member wants to contest what 
another member has said for its accurac y, the member should write to the Speaker. 
There is a procedure about that. 
CHRIS HIPKINS: I think the difficulty we have is that the senior Government whip 
has made an allegation about me by way of a point of order. 
I have now had the opportunity to consult the document that I tabled yesterday, and it

Both countries have a bilateral extradition treaty that forms the basis of their requests 
to each other. It is important to understand he re that extradition proceeds on the basis of 
a record of the case—that is, that the US provides a summary of the evidence 
supporting extradition and any other relevant materials. And then what the New Zealand 
court has to do is approach the record on the assumption that it is a fair and an accurate

Zealand to try the person for the offence alleged. Ultimately, if the extradition takes

It is also important to understand, which expl ains the detailed nature of extradition,

This legislation is required to complete the memorial in time for the centenary of the 
Gallipoli landings, and this very speedy prog ression will enable Government agencies 
to start work in October on what will be New Zealand’s major legacy project for the 
First World War commemorations: this wonderf ul park, Pukeahu. It is the centrepiece 
of the Government’s programme of projects and activities to mark the centenary over 
the 2014-18 period. The joint agency WW100 Programme Office in the Ministry for 
Culture and Heritage is going to lead a nd facilitate commemorative activities in 
accordance with other organisations of the Crown like the New Zealand Defence Force, 
the Department of Internal Affairs, the Mi nistry of Foreign A ffairs and Trade, and 
others, and a panel of trusted New Zealande rs is going to be guiding and informing 
these activities. During this period the war memorial is very much going to be a focus of 
the First World War commemorations and also , increasingly, of a number of significant 
70th anniversaries of the Second World War and, as time progresses, of anniversaries for 
both the Viet Nam and Korean wars. This bill is going to ensure that we have a park that 
provides a more appropriate setting for these very important commemorative activities. 
 What the bill does is it grants resource consents, heritage authorisations, and 
building consents, and provides for the desi gnation of the land, and powers of entry on 
to the land. It grants rights to the Mini stry for Culture and Heritage and the New 
Zealand Transport Agency to complete th e undergrounding of State Highway 1 and the 
memorial park in time for the centenary of the Gallipoli landings in April 2015. In 
doing so, what it is going to do is remove th e standard objection and appeal rights 
available under the Resource Management Act 1991, the Historic Places Act 1993, and 
the Public Works Act 1981, but I emphasise th at rights to compensation under the latter 
Act are going to be preserved. And should the n eed arise, the bill will also enable the

Like many public memorials, the developm ent of this National War Memorial has 
proceeded in fits and starts. In the 1920s there was a debate over what form it should 
take. There was some talk that there coul d even be a memorial parade or a new 
cathedral, and then a Wellingt on jeweller, Mr Denton, suggested the Carillon with bells 
of remembrance, and that was the idea th at was enthusiastically embraced by the 
community. The Wellington War Memorial Cari llon Society raised the money for a 49-
bell carillon and presented the funds to the Government. The Government then made its 
contribution towards the construc tion of the bell towers to house the Carillon. Gummer 
and Ford were two persons who won the design competition for the bell tower and the 
new national museum behind it. Gummer was renowned for his work on memorials. I 
think he was responsible for the Massey Me morial on Watts Peninsula and the Bridge 
of Remembrance in Christchurch. And so it wa s in 1932 that the publ ic flocked to this 
new memorial. At last, New Zealanders had a surrogate tomb for the thousands who 
had, sadly, died overseas in service of their country. 
 The next stage was supposed to be an  adjoining Hall of Memories, but its 
construction was cut short be cause of the Depression and then the Second World War. 
Indeed, it was to be 32 years before that building was finally opened in 1964. In 2004 
Kingsley Baird’s Tomb of the Unknown Wa rrior was added to the complex, and the 
remains of an unnamed soldier from Caterp illar Valley Cemetery near Longueval were 
interred in the tomb.  
I give the House that history because it is im portant to recognise that this has been a 
developing project, but with this developmen t we will be able to say that we finally 
have a complete memorial to those who have  served this country so well. With the 
completion of the project, the impressive ar chitecture of the memorial is going to be 
complemented by a park of equivalent  substance and design. The National War 
Memorial and the various elements of the pr ecinct will be unified. It is going to be a 
place of quiet reflection where people can congregate for important national 
commemorations, and our allies will also be  honoured with their own memorials. I 
emphasise that there is also going to be an interpretation centre, where young New 
Zealanders who attend Anzac Day commemorations will be able to learn more about the 
tumultuous events that have left their mark  on this country. So too will visitors to 
Wellington from around the country and overseas be drawn to the memorial.  
In the future, I believe the pr ecinct is most likely to be included in the Government’s 
proposed national historic landm ark list of places that are significant national treasures 
to New Zealand. Last but not least, the tr affic noise is going to be greatly reduced

Hon SIMON BRIDGES (Minister of Consumer Affairs)  on behalf of the 
Minister of Commerce: I move, That the Commerce (Inter national Co-operation, and 
Fees) Amendment Bill, the Credit Contract s and Consumer Finan ce (International Co-
operation) Amendment Bill, the Fair Tradi ng (International Co-operation) Amendment 
Bill, and the Telecommunications (International  Co-operation) Amendment Bill be now 
read a third time . The legislation plays an important role in supporting the 
Government’s objective of a single economic market with Australia. It builds on other 
single economic market initiatives progres sed by the Government over the past 12 
months, such as the Trans-Tasman Proceedings Act. The aim of this legislation is to 
facilitate enhanced cooperation between the Commerce Commission and the Australian 
Competition and Consumer Commission and ot her overseas competition and consumer 
regulators. The legislation aims to achie ve this by enabling the Commerce Commission 
to use its statutory powers and information acquired through use of its statutory powers 
to assist the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and overseas regulators 
in other countries. This in turn should enhance the commission’s ability to obtain 
assistance from overseas regulators for its own investigations.  
I would like to quickly outline some of the key features of the regime in the 
legislation. Firstly, the proposed amendments  operate on the princi ple of reciprocity. 
This should ensure that cooperation arrangements under the legislation result in benefits 
to New Zealand. Secondly, the legislation provi des flexibility in the type of cooperation 
arrangements to be used. By allowing both Government to Government and regulator to 
regulator types of agreements , it allows us to tailor our  approach to cooperation 
agreements with different c ountries as is appropriate. Thirdly, and very important, 
although the regime enhances the commission’ s ability to assist overseas competition 
and consumer regulators, it re cognises that in doing so ther e need to be appropriate 
public interest safeguards.  
The legislation provides such safeguards at  two levels. Firstly, it does so through 
requiring specific matters to be taken into account at a ministerial level. Such matters 
are broad, and include having regard to the legal framework in the overseas country and 
the potential consequences to New Zealand businesses and consumers of a cooperation 
arrangement. Secondly, and separately, once a cooperation arrangement is in place, the 
legislation requires specific matters to be considered by the co mmission on a case by 
case basis. Providing safeguards at both levels is important in ensuring that appropriate 
consideration is given to pub lic interest matters at diffe rent stages. It should also 
promote confidence in the integrity and implementation of cooperation arrangements 
under the legislation.  
Overall, the legislation further implements the Government’s commitment to making 
further progress towards a si ngle economic market with Au stralia. In doing so, the 
legislation equips the commission with modern-day tools to combat anti-competitive 
behaviour and enforce consumer laws in the international context of business today.  
I would like to thank everyone who has cont ributed to the legi slation, including the 
members of the Commerce Committee, the Parl iamentary Counsel Office, officials, and 
the members of the public and industry representatives who participated in the various 
submission and policy processes. I want also  to acknowledge other parties in the House 
for their support of this legislation.  
I commend these bills to the House, and move that they be read a third time.
